title: Basic statistics
text:
For a large majority of researchers, statistics is often reduced to selecting the correct statistical test and checking whether the resulting \(p\)-value meets the threshold for statistical significance. Under this mindset, an empirical study can feel fruitless if its results fail to achieve statistical significance.
Despite persistent efforts by statisticians to warn against the misuse of \(p\)-values and Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST), and despite the introduction of alternative metrics, standard testing practices remain deeply entrenched. This reductionist approach obscures the core philosophy of statistical thinking, perpetuates misunderstanding, and in some cases, methodological malpractices.
To build an intuitive understanding of statistics, the discipline can be divided into two main areas1:
This half version focuses primarily on descriptive statistics, while inferential statistics—which requires a deeper mathematical background—will be covered in future release. Nevertheless, mathematical concepts and notation remain essential throughout this section. Readers seeking clarification on foundational notation are encouraged to review the preceding section on basic mathematics.
To touch on a familiar perspective, Mark Twain famously popularized the phrase: “There are three kinds of lies: lies, damned lies, and statistics.” This quote highlights how easily statistical presentation can be manipulated. On one end of the spectrum, individuals without statistical training may accept any presented number as absolute proof. On the other end, someone well-versed in statistics can intentionally transform data or cherry-pick tests to support a desired conclusion.
The section begins laying foundation of the statistical framework by defining a population (15  Population) as the fundamental unit of study, and a variable (16  Variable) as a function mapping a domain (the population) to a codomain (the observed values). From this perspective, the distinction between quantitative (17  Quantitative variable) and qualitative (18  Qualitative variable) variables depends directly on the mathematical properties of the codomain.
The remaining chapters cover data first level- and second-level summary of the data. A first-level summary focuses on representing raw sequences of values as distributions such as bar charts and histograms (19  Distribution) and cumulative distributions (20  Cumulative distribution).
The second-level description focuses on condensing the first-level summary (distributions) into single metrics: measures of central tendency, including the mean (21  Arithmetic mean), median (24  Median), and mode (22  Mode); and measures of dispersion, including variance and standard deviation (23  Variance and standard deviation). The section conclues with the concepts of quantiles or percentiles (25  Quantile).

text:
Formal
The three questions above illustrate how calculating an average age depends on the specific population being studied. Without a clearly defined population, the question becomes meaningless, as the answer hinges on who is being studied. When researchers describe their work, they often mention the species and location—such as lemurs in Ranomafana or chameleons in Ambohitantely—which effectively identifies their population of interest.
In practice, the exact answers to these questions cannot be determined because it is practically impossible to collect age data from every single individual in a population. Instead, researchers select a sample from the population, calculate its mean, and use that result to approximate the average of the entire group.
Many terms used in statistics are borrowed from everyday language, and population is one of them. A subtle aim of this book is to highlight the subtle differences between how these terms are used in common speech versus how they are defined scientifically. To state the obvious, a population does not refer only to humans; and to state the less obvious, a sample is not the population.
A population is a collection of items under study. It can be categorized using two rigorous sub-definitions:
While both types are introduced here for completeness1, this section focuses on the first sub-definition. The second will be revisited later in the context of more advanced concepts.

title: 15  Population
text:
Tangible (or Existent) Population: A concrete, finite set of existing elements, denoted by a finite index set \(P=\{1,2, \ldots, N\}\).
Hypothetical Population: An infinite set of all possible outcomes that could be generated by a repeatable experiment, such as an infinite sequence of coin tosses, represented mathematically by its probability distribution.

title: 15  Population
text:
Examples

Passengers of the Titanic: One of the few examples where a complete database exists, allowing us to “know” every individual.
Students in a single classroom: the average grade is known, not need to estimate.
An endangered species endemic to a single location where every individual can be tagged and tracked. E.g., the endangered Saimaa ringed seals in Finland2.

title: 15  Population
text:
Tips and warnings

A population is a well-defined collection of items but knowing precisely what is included and excluded is non-trivial. For example, when defining the Malagasy population, does it include foreign residents living in Madagascar? Do we exclude individuals in rural areas who lack birth certificates? And should Malagasy citizens living abroad be counted?
Defining what constitutes an single unit can also be complex. While straightforward for some many animals, it becomes less obvious in other cases. For instance, in grasses, what defines a single unit of population? Similarly, when studying eusocial insects like ants, is the individual ant the individual, or is it the entire colony?
In mathematics, a function is defined with respect to a domain and a codomain. For statistical rigor, the population serves a role similar to the domain.
Ultimately, defining a population is not the final goal; rather, it provides the framework required to study the characteristics of that population, such as its variables and distributions.

title: 16  Variable
text:
Formal
This section complements the previous one: to build our statistical framework—and formulate precise research questions—a paired set of concepts is needed. We must define both the population (Chapter 15) and the specific characteristics of that population.
On the surface, a variable is simply a characteristic or feature of interest. Standard textbooks often define it this way because the characteristic varies from one individual or item to another within a population. When working with tabular data in a data frame, a variable typically corresponds to a single column in long-format data.
However, taking a more critical view raises philosophical questions. What, precisely, is a variable? Is it the column header itself (such as “height”), or is it the set of values contained within that column? Are these two ideas identical?
Consider measuring student heights in a single classroom. Height could be collected by asking each student to self-report their height, or by measuring each student directly with a tape measure. Because the measurement methods differ, do these two approaches yield the same variable or two distinct ones? If both methods happen to produce identical values for every student, are the variables then considered identical?
The clearest way to resolve these questions is to define a variable by its measurement process, rather than viewing it merely as a collection of numbers. In statistical terms, a variable is fundamentally a function (Chapter 8). For any mathematical function to be well-defined, it requires a domain, an assignment rule, and a codomain. In statistics, the domain \(X\) represents the population (or sample) under study, the function \(f\) represents the measurement method, and the codomain \(Y\) represents the set of resulting values that populate the data column.
Viewing variables through this functional lens makes classification straightforward. Whether a variable is qualitative (Chapter 18), quantitative (Chapter 17), discrete, or continuous (Chapter 3) depends directly on the properties of its codomain.
A variable in statistics is a characteristic, attribute, or property of an individual item or subject in a population that can take on different values across different observations.
In formal terms1, if a population or sample is represented as a set of entities \(\Omega\), a variable \(X\) is defined as a function:
\[X: \Omega \rightarrow \mathcal{V}\]
where:

title: 16  Variable
text:
\(\Omega\) is the domain, representing the set of items, subjects, or experimental units under study.
\(\mathcal{V}\) is the codomain (or state space), representing the set of all permissible values that the variable can take.
\(X(\omega)\) assigns a specific measured or observed value in \(\mathcal{V}\) to a particular unit \(\omega \in \Omega\).

title: 16  Variable
text:
Examples
Below are examples of variables2

When the population consists of study sites: GPS coordinates, elevation, temperature, rainfall, humidity.
When the population is a village: age, social status, and sex.
When the population is plants: diameter at breast height (dbh), height, and growth measured between two time points.

title: 16  Variable
text:
Tips and warnings

Is a constant a variable? In practical terms, no, which is precisely why the term “variable” is used in the first place. However, if you measure a characteristic—such as religion in a classroom—expecting it to vary, but discover after collecting data that every individual shares the same religion, should it still be treated as a variable? In mathematics, a constant function like \(f(x) = 1\) is still a valid function. These edge cases could serve as an exercise to think critically about what defines a variable.
Variables are frequently transformed. For instance, a researcher might record age as a continuous numerical (Chapter 17) value and later categorize the data into age brackets like infant, juvenile, and adult (Chapter 18). Once transformed, it becomes a distinct variable with different properties.
A central concept in inferential statistics is the random variable. Its formal treatment is deferred until additional mathematical and statistical foundations are introduced (in future version).


Notation/Semantic/Terminology
Because this book navigates between three subjects—mathematics, statistics, and computer programming—terms with multiple meanings are unavoidable. “Variable” is the most critical example. In mathematics, a variable is an abstract symbol, such as \(x\) or \(y\), linked by a function \(f\). In statistics, it is formalised as a function tied to a specific population and set of measurements. In computer programming, it represents a named reference to an object in memory via variable assignment (Chapter 29).
Whether a variable is described as independent, dependent, or a response variable relates to its role in a relationship—specifically, whether it acts as part of the domain (source set) or the codomain (target set). In contrast, classifying a variable as qualitative, quantitative, discrete, continuous, or boolean reflects the structural properties of the target set itself.

title: 17  Quantitative variable
text:
Formal
A quantitative variable is a function that maps an element of a population to a numerical value (Chapter 16). Working with quantitative variables feels natural, as it aligns with the standard mathematics and physics covered throughout secondary education. Difficulties typically arise when dealing with qualitative variables (Chapter 18)—specifically, confusing qualitative variables with quantitative ones, conflating discrete variables with qualitative ones, or inappropriately applying quantitative tools to qualitative data. These distinctions are addressed in the next section (Chapter 18).
The fundamental distinction rests on the two main categories of numbers: discrete and continuous (Chapter 3). Consequently, there are two corresponding types of quantitative variables based on whether the codomain contains discrete values (such as integers) or continuous values.
The divide between discrete and continuous variables becomes critical when studying probability distributions, statistical inference, and model fitting, primarily because the underlying mathematical machinery required to analyze them differs significantly (Chapter 3)—a topic deferred again to a future version.
In basic descriptive statistics, whether a variable is discrete or continuous rarely alters the computation of summary statistics such as the mean (Chapter 21) or variance (Chapter 23).
A quantitative variable in statistics is a characteristic of an individual unit in a population that takes on numerical values across observations1.
Quantitative variables are classified into two main types:

title: 17  Quantitative variable
text:
A quantitative variable is discrete if its set of possible values is countable, typically consisting of isolated points on a number line (Chapter 3).
A quantitative variable is continuous if its set of possible values forms an unbroken interval of real numbers. It can take on any value within that interval, constrained only by the precision of the measuring instrument (e.g., the height of a student measured at 1.65 m).

title: 17  Quantitative variable
text:
Examples
Below are examples of discrete and continuous variables across different fields. In practice, the underlying population must be defined for these measurement to hold.
Zoological2 metrics:

Continuous: weight, height, snout-to-vent length, personal income, grade point average, total surface area of an apartment owned, total land area owned.
Discrete: number of offspring, number of limbs, number of cows owned.

Botanical metrics:

Continuous: diameter at breast height (dbh), plant height, wood hardness.
Discrete: life stage defined by the number of nodes in maize, number of trifoliates in soybean.

Landscape metrics:

Continuous: population density, elevation, landscape connectivity, distance to the nearest habitat patch.
Discrete: number of individuals in a fragment, number of females in a population.

title: 17  Quantitative variable
text:
Tips and warnings

A useful rule of thumb: a variable is quantitative if applying standard arithmetic operations (Chapter 1) to its values yields a meaningful result.
Quantitative variables are frequently transformed; common transformations include log scaling (Chapter 12), square root transformations, and centering (subtracting each value by the mean).
Beware of “fake” quantitative variables. Identifiers such as ZIP codes or phone numbers consist of digits, but they are not quantitative. Adding or averaging two ZIP codes (e.g., Tana 101 and Ambalavao 303) produces no meaningful mathematical interpretation; the numbers serve merely as convenient categorical labels.
While discrete quantitative variables consist of integers, qualitative variables has the property of being discrete in the sense that their categories can be indexed by integers. But qualitative variable are not discrete variable.
A quantitative variable can take positive, negative, or zero values; sign does not affect whether a variable is discrete or continuous. Because discrete variables are often used for counting, they are frequently non-negative.
In taxonomy, count variables (such as the number of floral parts) are sometimes used to classify species. In this context, the population of interest consists of species rather than individual organisms.


Semantic/Terminology/Notation

The statistical term discrete is unrelated to the French term “être discret”.
Terminology varies across disciplines. Continuous variables are called real numbers (\(\mathbb{R}\)) in mathematics, called numeric in data science, and float or double data types in computer programming.

title: 18  Qualitative variable
text:
Formal
This chapter builds directly on the preceding material: a qualitative variable is defined simply as any variable that is NOT quantitative (Chapter 17)
There is an inherent paradox in how we understand and use qualitative variables. On one hand, the human brain has a natural propensity to categorize the world: male or female, good or bad, species classifications, or the establishment of national borders. We naturally think in qualitative terms. On the other hand, the foundational tools of mathematics and statistics are built around numbers and arithmetic operations. This creates friction, as it is not immediately obvious what statistical operations apply when observations are non-numerical.
Categorical variables with clear-cut boundaries—such as sex, eye color, or species—rarely cause confusion. Ambiguity arises primarily when qualitative variables are derived from underlying quantitative variables. This fuzziness occurs for two reasons: researchers often lose sight of the original quantitative measurement, and the boundaries used to define the categories are inherently arbitrary. Consider the categories infant, juvenile, and adult: while the underlying variable is continuous age, there is no single universal rule for where one stage ends and the next begins1. Similarly, classifying locations into low, intermediate, or high elevation relies on continuous altitude, yet the specific cutoffs chosen are largely contextual.
A final common misconception is confusing qualitative variables with assessments of quality. In statistical practice, “qualitative” refers strictly to membership in a category, not value judgments. Replacing the term qualitative variable with categorical variable clears up this confusion2.
A qualitative variable in statistics is a characteristic of an individual unit in a population that takes on non-numerical values across observations3.
Qualitative variables are divided into three main types: nominal, ordinal, and binary.

title: 18  Qualitative variable
text:
A nominal variable consists of categories with no inherent ordering (e.g., eye color, species, or country of origin).
An ordinal variable possesses a natural sequence or rank among its categories (e.g., infant, juvenile, adult). Note that many ordinal variables are created by binning an underlying continuous quantitative variable (Chapter 17).
A binary variable is a special case of a qualitative variable that contains exactly two mutually exclusive categories (e.g., yes/no, true/false, or 0/1) (Chapter 33).

title: 18  Qualitative variable
text:
Examples
Below are examples illustrating the distinct categories of qualitative variables:

Nominal variables:

Nationality (e.g., Malagasy, English, Kenyan)
Political affiliation (e.g. TGV, TIM, AREMA, MONIMA)
Eye color (e.g., blue, brown, green)
Species name (e.g., Lemur catta, Panthera leo)
ZIP code (e.g., 101, 102, 303)
Notice that while ZIP codes consist of numbers, a ZIP code is a nominal variable rather than a quantitative one. Applying arithmetic operations to ZIP codes yields no mathematical meaning; the numbers serve merely as categorical labels.

Ordinal variables with implicit ordering:

Education level (e.g., High School, Bachelor’s, Master’s, PhD)
Customer satisfaction (e.g., Very Dissatisfied, Dissatisfied, Neutral, Satisfied, Very Satisfied)
Egg size classification (e.g., Small, Medium, Large, Extra Large)

In these cases, ratings or sizes are assigned to discrete categories without measuring an exact underlying numerical continuum. Even if numeric codes are assigned to the categories (such as 1, 2, 3, 4), computing a standard arithmetic average remains conceptually invalid. However, the sequence preserves rank: a rating of 3 reflects higher satisfaction than a 2, and 2 reflects higher satisfaction than a 1.
Ordinal variables derived from an underlying quantitative continuum:

Age group (e.g., child, teenager, adult, senior; derived from age)
Income bracket (e.g., low, medium, high; derived from salary)
Academic grade category (e.g., fail, pass, distinction; derived from a numerical score)
Elevation zone (e.g., lowland, mid-altitude, highland; derived from altitude)

Binary variables:

Academic grade category (e.g., fail, pass, distinction; derived from a numerical score)
Sex (e.g., male, female)
Question outcomes with two options (e.g., Yes/No responses to “Do you own a car?”)

title: 18  Qualitative variable
text:
Tips and warnings

Flexibility of notation: A qualitative variable can be recorded using many different symbolic representations. For example, a binary survival status column can be coded as dead/alive, d/a, maty/velona, yes/no, Y/N, 1/0, or oui/non. It is crucial to distinguish between the underlying value or category and the notation used to represent it. Using numeric symbols like 1 and 0 does not make the variable quantitative; they remain shorthand representations for discrete categories. For true quantitative variables, by contrast, the numerical values are fixed by measurement and cannot be arbitrarily renamed.
Record quantitative data whenever possible: Collecting data in qualitative categories (such as age brackets) can be faster or easier in the field, but it involves a permanent loss of information. A continuous quantitative variable (like age in years) can always be binned into qualitative categories later, but qualitative categories cannot be converted back into precise quantitative measurements.
Visualization constraints: The structural nature of a variable dictates the appropriate visualization methods. For example, a histogram is strictly designed to show the continuous distribution of quantitative data, whereas qualitative data must be visualized using tools appropriate for counts across discrete categories, such as bar charts.
Encoding binary variables: Any binary qualitative variable can be reframed as a boolean (True/False) question. Instead of recording a variable named color with categories Blue or Red, one can define the variable as Is_Blue? with values True or False. Utilizing native boolean types is often computationally advantageous, as programming languages possess dedicated structures to handle two-state logic efficiently (Chapter 33).
These variables are not mutually exclusive. Ordinal variables can always be coerced into or considered as a nominal variable by ignoring the order. Whereas the reverse is not possible. It is not possible to order eye color per se. And any variable can always be coerced into a binary variable (blue eye and not blue eye). Binary variable can also be considered as nominal variable.

title: 19  Distribution
text:
Formal
There are two main entry points for understanding a statistical distribution. The first is theoretical, involving formal parametric distributions such as the Gaussian (Normal), Binomial, or Poisson distributions. That theoretical perspective will be deferred again to the next version.
The second entry point, descriptive statistics, is empirical or data-driven. Consider a qualitative variable (Chapter 18)—for example, observing the sex of all \(n\) students in a classroom (where the variable \(X\) maps a population \(\Omega\) to a state space \(\mathcal{V}\), see Chapter 16 and Chapter 15). The raw data is simply a sequence of observations (e.g., male, female, female, male…). A distribution serves as the primary tool for summarizing this raw data by calculating summary metrics from the original observations.
To construct this summary for qualitative variable, one counts the frequency of observations in each category. The raw sequence of categories is thereby transformed into a frequency table:
Visually, this categorical distribution is represented as a bar plot featuring two bars whose heights correspond to \(n_m\) and \(n_f\).
While this process is straightforward for qualitative data, a question arises: how does one construct a tabular data and visual distribution for continuous quantitative variables (Chapter 17)? If student heights are also measured, the result is a sequence of \(n\) real numbers. If one attempts to tabulate frequencies by unique numerical values, the resulting table becomes an unwieldy set of single-instance counts, yielding a plot of uniformly thin bars with a height of 1—offering little to no analytical insight.
To meaningfully visualize such a continuous sequence, the quantitative values are binned into an ordinal qualitative variable. Similar to grouping continuous altitude measurements into elevation zones, binning continuous data reduces the number of table columns to a manageable set of intervals (bins) with meaningful count frequencies.
However, interval selection is inherently subjective. The resulting empirical distribution and its corresponding table depend directly on the chosen bin boundaries. For instance, if exam scores range continuously from 0 to 20, one could define two broad intervals—\([0, 10)\)1 and \([10, 20]\)—or divide the domain into four equal intervals: \([0, 5)\), \([5, 10)\), \([10, 15)\), and \([15, 20]\). Because different binning choices alter the visual profile of the distribution, the rationale behind the chosen interval widths must always be explicitly stated.
In summary, while a variable consists of an observed sequence of values, its empirical distribution transforms that sequence into paired discrete bins and corresponding frequency counts. Visualizing these counts (Chapter 9) reveals not only the most and least frequent values, but also the overall density and dispersion of the entire dataset.
A distribution is a tabular or visual summary of a variable’s observed values—whether recorded as a sequence of numbers or discrete categories—constructed by counting the frequency of occurrences across the data (see Chapter 9 for the equivalence between pairs of number and the visual representations).
By mapping raw observations to their respective counts or proportions, a distribution converts unstructured sequence data into a structured format.
An empirical frequency distribution can be formalized either through a binned domain (partitioned intervals) or directly over individual observed values.
Read this first2

title: 19  Distribution
text:
Pointwise Definition (Value-Based)
The empirical frequency distribution can be defined directly on individual observed values.
For any unique value \(x \in \Omega\), the absolute empirical frequency function \(n(x)\) and relative empirical frequency function \(f(x)\) are given by:
\[n(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{I}(x_i = x) \quad \text{and} \quad f(x) = \frac{n(x)}{n}\]
In operational terms, \(n(x)\) counts the exact number of occurrences of the specific outcome \(x\), while \(f(x)\) represents the proportion of the total sample equal to \(x\).


Binned Definition (Interval-Based)
Let \(\{B_j\}_{j=1}^K\) be an ordered partition of the observed sample domain into \(K\) mutually disjoint bins:
\[B_j \cap B_k = \emptyset \quad \forall \, j \neq k\]
where the bins respect a strict linear ordering: if \(j < k\), then \(x < y\) for all \(x \in B_j\) and \(y \in B_k\).
For any bin index \(j \in \{1, 2, \dots, K\}\), the absolute frequency \(n(B_j)\) and relative frequency \(f(B_j)\) are defined respectively as:
\[n(B_j) = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{I}(x_i \in B_j) \quad \text{and} \quad f(B_j) = \frac{n(B_j)}{n}\]
where \(\mathbb{I}(\cdot)\) is the indicator function evaluating to \(1\) if the condition holds and \(0\) otherwise, and \(n\) represents the total sample size.


Fundamental Property
An immediate mathematical consequence of these definitions is normalization: summing all relative frequencies across the domain equals unity:
\[\sum_{j=1}^K f(B_j) = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad \sum_{x \in \mathbb{R}} f(x) = 1\]

The first figure illustrates distributions for qualitative variables. For nominal qualitative variables, the ordering of categories along the horizontal axis is arbitrary; reordering the categories (e.g., placing species in ascending or descending frequency order) alters the visual layout but leaves the underlying empirical distribution unchanged.

Comparing the two histograms demonstrates how interval size alters visualization: a coarse bin width (\(\Delta x = 1.0\)) smooths over local variation to highlight overall shape, whereas a finer bin width (\(\Delta x = 0.2\)) reveals finer structural details and sampling noise.

title: 19  Distribution
text:
Tips and warnings

Bar charts vs. histograms: A bar chart is strictly designed for qualitative (categorical) variables, where discrete categories are visually separated by spaces to emphasize their independence and non-continuous nature. In contrast, a histogram is reserved for continuous quantitative variables, where adjacent bars touch to represent contiguous numerical intervals (bins). Bin selection in a histogram explicitly defines the width and boundaries of these intervals, directly shaping how continuous data is discretized for visualization.
For nominal qualitative variables, category order along the horizontal axis is arbitrary, unless the variable is ordinal. A standard practice for nominal data is to sort categories by frequency (ascending or descending). This reordering significantly improves visual interpretation by making relative rank and magnitude differences instantly clear.











The vertical axis of an empirical distribution can be scaled in multiple ways depending on the analytical goal. Common y-axis representations include absolute counts, relative counts (proportions), and probability density (where the total area of the bars equals 1). Selecting an appropriate vertical scaling depends primarily on the context of interpretation: for instance, when comparing distributions across groups with unequal sample sizes (n), relative frequencies or probability densities provide a common baseline that raw absolute counts fail to offer.









Figure 19.4: Comparison of empirical distribution scale representations: absolute count, relative frequency, and probability density.






Smooth curves—such are also used to represent empirical data-driven distributions. Constructing these continuous representations requires additional analytical machinery, such as kernel selection and bandwidth optimization. While smooth density curves provide an intuitive and aesthetically pleasing overview of continuous data, they can easily mislead if over-smoothed, masking true multimodal patterns or obscuring local variation in small samples.
The concept of a distribution is the fundamental cornerstone of statistics, bridging theoretical probability and empirical data analysis.

title: 20  Cumulative distribution
text:
Formal
Cumulative mass and density functions offer an alternative, complementary representation of the empirical distribution (Chapter 19) for quantitative variables (Chapter 17) and ordinal qualitative variables (Chapter 18). While the terms cumulative mass function (CMF) and cumulative density function (CDF) originate from theoretical probability, their empirical data-driven logic is straightforward.
For a given absolute bin frequencies \[f_1, f_2, f_3, \dots, f_n,\] the corresponding cumulative frequencies are computed sequentially as \(c_1 = f_1\), \(c_2 = f_1 + f_2\), more generally \[c_k = \sum_{i=1}^k f_i.\] A cumulative distribution contains identical information to its standard frequency counterpart; the cumulative values \(c_k\) are derived by summing frequencies \(f_i\), and the original frequencies \(f_i\) can be fully recovered via successive differencing (\(f_i = c_i - c_{i-1}\)).
For an ordinal variable, cumulative frequencies reflect the total count of observations falling at or below a given ordered category. The side-by-side bar plots below compare a standard frequency distribution with its cumulative stacked representation.
For continuous quantitative variables, the cumulative empirical distribution tracks the running tally of observations accumulated across contiguous measurement intervals. Side-by-side comparison demonstrates how individual bin frequencies map directly to the monotonically increasing shape of the cumulative histogram.
The empirical cumulative distribution can be formalized either through a binned domain (partitioned intervals) or directly over individual observed values.
Read this first1

title: 20  Cumulative distribution
text:
Pointwise Definition (Value-Based)
The cumulative empirical distribution can be defined directly on individual observed values .
With an ordered set \(\Omega\), for any value \(x \in \Omega\), the absolute empirical cumulative distribution function \(N(x)\) and relative empirical cumulative distribution function \(F(x)\) are given by:
\[N(x) = \sum_{x_i \le x} n(x_i) \quad \text{and} \quad F(x) = \sum_{x_i \le x} f(x_i)\]
where \(n(x_i)\) is the absolute frequency of the unique value \(x_i\), and \(f(x_i) = \dfrac{n(x_i)}{n}\) is its relative frequency. In operational terms, \(F(x)\) sums the relative frequencies of all observed outcomes less than or equal to \(x\).


Binned Definition (Interval-Based)
Let \(\{B_j\}_{j=1}^K\) be an ordered partition of the observed sample domain into \(K\) mutually disjoint bins:
\[B_j \cap B_k = \emptyset \quad \forall \, j \neq k\]
where the bins respect a strict linear ordering: if \(j < k\), then \(x < y\) for all \(x \in B_j\) and \(y \in B_k\).
For any bin index \(i \in \{1, 2, \dots, K\}\), the absolute cumulative frequency \(N(i)\) and relative cumulative frequency \(F(i)\) are defined respectively as:
\[N(i) = \sum_{j=1}^i n(B_j) \quad \text{and} \quad F(i) = \sum_{j=1}^i f(B_j)\]
where \(n(B_j)\) is the absolute count of observations in bin \(B_j\), and \(f(B_j) = \dfrac{n(B_j)}{n}\) is the corresponding relative frequency for a sample size \(n\).


Fundamental Property
An immediate mathematical consequence of these definitions is monotonicity: both \(N(x)\) and \(F(x)\) are non-decreasing functions over their respective domains:
\[x_a \le x_b \implies F(x_a) \le F(x_b)\]

title: 20  Cumulative distribution
text:
Examples

For discrete quantitative variables, a cumulative distribution is visualized using a lollipop plot with cumulative counts. Aligning the y-axis scales (\(0\) to \(n\)) highlights how frequencies accumulate step-by-step across discrete values until reaching the total sample size.











For a uniform flat distribution, the frequency of observations are spread evenly across all bins, the cumulative histogram rises at a constant rate, producing a straight linear slope.











When data is concentrated near smaller values, cumulative counts rise steeply early on before flattening out as values become sparse.

title: 20  Cumulative distribution
text:
Tips and warnings

Cumulative distributions rely on a natural, well-defined ordering along the horizontal axis. For nominal qualitative variables, category ordering is arbitrary; rearranging the categories yields entirely different cumulative sequences, making a unique cumulative representation impossible. However, ordinal qualitative variables (Chapter 18) possess a meaningful inherent ranking and can be validly expressed cumulatively.
Expressing cumulative distributions in terms of relative frequencies or proportions rather than raw counts scales the vertical axis strictly from \(0\) to \(1\). This normalization eliminates dependence on sample size (\(n\)), permitting direct comparisons between datasets of different sizes.
Cumulative distributions provide a straightforward visual and numerical mechanism for locating quantiles, such as the median (Chapter 24) or arbitrary quantiles (Chapter 25). By drawing a horizontal line from the vertical axis (e.g., at \(0.5\) or \(50\%\)) to the cumulative curve and projecting down to the horizontal axis, the corresponding quantile value can be identified.



From a theoretical perspective, cumulative functions are monotonically non-decreasing, bounded functions. This structural regularity makes them far easier for statisticians to manipulate mathematically, prove asymptotic properties, and utilize in non-parametric testing frameworks (e.g., the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).

title: 21  Arithmetic mean
text:
Formal
The mean is likely the most familiar concepts in statistics. Almost everyone knows how to calculate the average of numbers: “the sum of all values divided by the total count.” Yet, when presented with the formal mathematical equation (see Equation 21.2 and Equation 21.3), the confidence is lost. Hopefully, these formulas should be less daunting after reading Chapter 4 on mathematical notation.
There are three main ways to calculate the mean. The simple “sum divided by count” is the standard practical method. A second method applies when weights or coefficients are involved, such as with course grades. In that case, you multiply each grade by its coefficient, sum those products, and divide the total by the sum of all coefficients.
The third and most general formula multiplies each value by its relative frequency of occurrence and sums the results. In the grades example, instead of dividing by the sum of coefficients at the end, one multiplies each grade by its proportion of the total weight. This general approach allows to calculate the mean directly from a distribution (Chapter 19).
While the mean is the most common metric used to summarize data, reducing a set of numbers to a single value means losing helpful details. For instance, a student with test scores of 10/20 and 10/20 has the exact same average as a student with 5/20 and 15/20, even though their performance are completely different. Being the most common summary metric does not make the mean the best or the only option for every situation.
Here are three equations for calculating the mean. If the values are denoted by \(x_i\) and there are \(n\) observations, the familiar formula is:
\[
   \bar{X} = \mu = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i
\tag{21.1}\]
The second formula is similar; if \(x_i\) repeats \(n_i\) times () with \(\sum n_i = n\), the equation for the mean is:
\[
    \mu = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i} n_i \, x_i
\tag{21.2}\]
The third and general formula is obtained by multiplying each \(x_i\) by \(p_i = \pfrac{n_i}{n}\):
\[
    \mu = \sum_{i} p_i \, x_i
\tag{21.3}\]
In other words, the \(n\) outside the \(\sum\) in Equation 21.2 is distributed inside the summation symbol \(\sum\).

title: 21  Arithmetic mean
text:
Examples
Assume the grades of six students in a class are: \(\{5, 7, 10, 10, 12, 14\}\). Below are three formulas to calculate the mean :

\(\dfrac{5 + 7 + 10 + 10 + 12 + 14}{6}\)
\(\dfrac{1 \times 5 + 1 \times 7 + 2 \times 10 + 1 \times 12 + 1 \times 14}{6}\)
\(\dfrac{1}{6} \times 5 + \dfrac{1}{6} \times 7 + \dfrac{2}{6} \times 10 + \dfrac{1}{6} \times 12 + \dfrac{1}{6} \times 14\)

title: 21  Arithmetic mean
text:
Tips and warnings

The mean serves as a primary summary metric designed to capture the central tendency of a dataset, it is the center of mass (or gravity) of the data.
The arithmetic mean is only valid for quantitative variables otherwise (\(n_i \times x_i\) or \(\sum x_i\)) is not defined (Chapter 17)
The mean is highly sensitive to outliers or extreme skewness. For instance, computing the mean of the sequence \((1, 1, 1, 1, 10\,000\,000)\) yields \(2\,000\,000.4\), beyond the numerical value, it does not have a practical intepretation.
Averaging can yield incorrect conclusions when dealing with rates or ratios. For example, if you travel from Fianarantsoa to Ambalavao covering equal distances at \(30\text{ km/h}\) and \(60\text{ km/h}\), your overall average speed is not \(\frac{30 + 60}{2} = 45\text{ km/h}\).1
There are alternative definitions to calculate the mean (geometric and harmonic mean). In the speed example above, calculating the harmonic mean provides the correct average speed2.
When the distribution is perfectly symmetric (where the left side of the distribution mirrors the right), the center of gravity of the point symmetry is thus is the mean.


Notation/Semantic/Terminology

mean and average are synonymous, referring to the arithmetic measure of central location .
In probability theory and inferential statistics, the theoretical counterpart of the empirical mean is the expected value or expectation, denoted as \(\mathbb{E}[X]\). If dealing with a population Chapter 15, they are the same. But when sampling is involved, the empirical mean (\(\bar{X}\)) is an estimate of the population mean.
In mathematics, the mean is formalised as the first moment (often written as \(\mu_1\) or \(\mathbb{E}[X^1]\)). Higher-order moments describe other structural properties of a distribution—such as variance (second central moment) and skewness (third standardized moment).

title: 22  Mode
text:
Formal
In French, la mode (feminine) means fashion, while le mode (masculine) refers to the statistical mode. Yet, fashion is precisely the concept behind the statistical mode1. Conceptually, the statistical mode simply represents the most popular category, closely reflecting its everyday meaning. Looking at a distribution (Chapter 19), its interpretation is straightforward: it is the value or category with the highest frequency.
The mode is one of three main metrics used to measure central tendency, along with the mean (Chapter 21) and the median (Chapter 24). Unlike the mean and median, the mode works for qualitative and quantitative variables, and it is especially useful for the former. While most people are accustomed to calculating the mean, computing the mode is less common in daily life. Nevertheless, it is easy to identify from a distribution (Chapter 19).
The mode is the value that appears most often in a dataset. If \(X\) is a qualitative or discrete variable, the mode is the value \(x\) with the highest frequency of occurrence. For a continuous variable, the mode corresponds to the bin with the highest frequency, which means the exact mode depends on the choice of bin size and boundaries.
A mode does not have to be unique. Distributions can have multiple local peak values, leading to bimodal or multimodal distributions.
Finally, in the rare case where a distribution is completely flat—meaning all values occur with the exact same frequency—the mode does not exist.

title: 22  Mode
text:
Examples
The mode is generally inferred directly from a visual distribution.

For categorical/qualitative variables: Mouse is the single mode (unimodal) on the left, whereas both catta and mouse are modes (bimodal) on the right.











For discrete variables: The mode is 4, as it has the highest count.











More care is needed when identifying the mode of a continuous variable from a histogram. Because bin widths and boundaries are arbitrary, different binning choices can alter which bin appears as the mode.

title: 22  Mode
text:
Tips and warnings

The mode equals the mean and median only when the distribution is symmetric and unimodal, such as in a standard bell-shaped curve.
There is a common rule of thumb stating that for a right-skewed distribution, mode > median > mean (and the reverse for a left-skewed distribution). While useful to know theoretically, this relationship has little practical application.
Always inspect the distribution before running statistical tests, as most standard tests are not designed for multimodal data. If a distribution is bimodal or multimodal, special analytical steps must be taken.

title: 23  Variance and standard deviation
text:
Formal
Almost everyone has calculated an average grade, yet checking the variance of those grades is rarely considered. While calculating the mean is well understood, the formulas for variance and standard deviation are often forgotten.
When conducting statistical tests, analyzing variance becomes necessary—often without a clear understanding of why. Concepts such as homogeneity of variance or homoscedasticity can seem overly complex, largely because variance is routinely ignored in everyday calculations.
Due to the familiarity and utility of the mean, comparing two single numbers is easy, which often leads to the implicit assumption that the underlying distributions are identical. However, a single mean does not fully describe a distribution, as demonstrated below by three distinct distributions sharing the exact same mean.
Conversely, no one would conclude that equal variances imply identical distributions. Comparing distributions effectively is often achieved through a parsimonious approach that examines both the mean and the variance1. The mean indicates the central tendency, whereas the variance measures the dispersion. For well-behaved distributions—particularly those that are unimodal and symmetrical—these two metrics serve as the primary criteria for comparison.
In descriptive statistics, the equation for variance is:
\[
  \text{Var}(X) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (X_i - \bar{X})^2
\tag{23.1}\]
This formula is similar to the mean, except that \(X_i\) is replaced by \((X_i - \bar{X})^2\), which represents the squared distance of each observation from the mean. Variance is therefore the average squared distance from the mean.
Through algebraic manipulation, the equation can also be expressed as:
\[
  \text{Var}(X) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i^2 - \bar{X}^2
\tag{23.2}\]
This alternative formula is often simpler for manual calculations, though both methods require minimal computational effort.
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance:
\[
  \sigma = \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)}
\tag{23.3}\]

title: 23  Variance and standard deviation
text:
Examples

For a trivial dataset \(X = \{1, 1, 1, 1\}\), the mean is \(\mu = 1\).
The variance is:
\[
\begin{align*}
  \sigma^2 & = \frac{1}{4}\left((1 - \mu)^2 + (1 - \mu)^2 + (1 - \mu)^2 + (1 - \mu)^2\right) \\
  & = \frac{1}{4} (0) \times 4 = 0
\end{align*}
\] This result is intutitive: because all values are identical, there is no dispersion, and the variance (and standard deviation) is zero.
Following the previous calculation of the mean (Chapter 21): The mean was:
\[\mu = \frac{1}{6} 5 + \frac{1}{6} 7 + \frac{2}{6} 10 + \frac{1}{6} 12 + \frac{1}{6} 14 = 9.67\]
The variance is calculated as:
\[
\begin{align*}
  \sigma^2  = &\frac{1}{6}(5 - \mu)^2 + \frac{1}{6}(7 - \mu)^2 +  \frac{2}{6}(10 - \mu)^2 + \\
    &  \frac{1}{6}(12 - \mu)^2 + \frac{1}{6}(14 - \mu)^2 \\
   = & 8.56
\end{align*}
\]
Consider two schools: in the first, all 20 students scored 10/20. In the second, half of the students scored 0/20 and the other half scored 20/20. Although both schools share an identical mean of 10/20, the first school has a variance of 0, whereas the second has a variance of 100. Evaluating the variance reveals differences between the two performance at the school that the mean alone fails to capture.

title: 23  Variance and standard deviation
text:
Tips and warnings

Calculating the mean of a single number is pointless, as is calculating the variance of only two numbers.
Because variance relies on squared values, taking the square root yields a more interpretable metric. For instance, a grade variance of 100 is difficult to interpret on a 0 to 20 scale. Taking the standard deviation (\(\sigma = \sqrt{100} = 10\)) returns the measure of dispersion to the original scale of the data.
In the formal definition shown in Equation 23.1, variance involves the squared distance from the mean, known as the second moment. Raising values to higher powers, such as \(X^3\), yields higher moments that describe additional geometric features of the distribution.
A normal distribution is fully characterized by two parameters: the mean and the variance. For distributions that are approximately normal, comparing these two metrics is sufficient to compare the entire underlying distributions.
Variance can be calculated using two main formulas: one in which the sum of squared deviations is divided by \(n\) (Equation 23.1), and another in which it is divided by \(n - 1\). Standard functions in R compute variance using the \(n - 1\) denominator. Division by \(n\) defines the population variance (Chapter 15), which represents complete population data (likely unknown). Division by \(n - 1\) defines the sample variance, providing an estimate of the unknown (true) population variance. Consequently, the \(n - 1\) formulation is the standard approach in empirical analysis.

title: 24  Median
text:
Formal
Linguists estimate that there are over 7,000 languages in the world. At one end of the spectrum, approximately 1.18 billion people speak1 Mandarin Chinese and 609 million speak Hindi. At the other end, some languages have as few as one known speaker, such as Taushiro in Peru and Kaixana in Brazil.
On average, a language is spoken by roughly 1 million people, but this metric can be misleading. The standard deviation is approximately 17.5 million, reflecting extreme variability across the dataset2. By contrast, the median is approximately 8,000 speakers per language.
Which metric is more useful depends on the perspective being highlighted. An argument for language preservation might emphasize the median, noting that approximately 3,500 languages are spoken by fewer than 8,000 people. Conversely, an argument minimizing the urgency of language endangerment might cite the mean, pointing out that, on average, a language has many speakers.
A central conundrum is whether to use the mean or the median when comparing distributions (see also Chapter 23). There is no single correct choice; rather, understanding the existence and behavior of a metric should lead to a more informed decision.
In descriptive statistics, the median is determined by ordering the data values in non-decreasing order:
\[x_{(1)} \le x_{(2)} \le \dots \le x_{(n)}\]
If the sample size \(n\) is odd, the median is the value located exactly in the middle of the ordered observations. If \(n\) is even, the median is the arithmetic mean of the two central observations.
Formally, the sample median \(\tilde{x}\) is defined as:
\[
    \tilde{x} = \begin{cases} x_{\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)} & \text{if } n \text{ is odd} \\[8pt] \frac{1}{2}\left(x_{\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)} + x_{\left(\frac{n}{2}+1\right)}\right) & \text{if } n \text{ is even} \end{cases}
\]

title: 24  Median
text:
Examples
The median, shown in bold, is identical for each of the following datasets:

\(\{1, 1, \mathbf{3}, 3, 3\}\)
\(\{1, 2, \mathbf{3}, 4, 5\}\)
\(\{1, 3, \mathbf{3}, 10, 1000\}\)
\(\{-100, 1, \mathbf{3}, 3, 5\}\)
\(\{-1, -1, -1, -1, \mathbf{3}, 4, 5, 6, 101\}\)

For an even number of observations, the median is calculated as the average of the two middle values:

\(\{1, 1, 3, 3\} \rightarrow \text{median} = \frac{1 + 3}{2} = 2\)
\(\{1, 2, 3, 4\} \rightarrow \text{median} = \frac{2 + 3}{2} = 2.5\)
\(\{1, 3, 3, 10\} \rightarrow \text{median} = \frac{3 + 3}{2} = 3\)
\(\{-100, 1, 3, 3\} \rightarrow \text{median} = \frac{1 + 3}{2} = 2.0\)

The diffifult aspect of determining the median by hand is the tedious part of ordering the values.

title: 24  Median
text:
Tips and warnings

The median is the primary measure of central tendency used in boxplots.
A major advantage of the median compared to the mean is its resistance to extreme values and outliers. Whether this property is desirable depends on the context.
If unsure, calculating both the mean and the median allows for an assessment of how much they diverge and how that difference might influence conclusions.
Part of learning statistics is understanding the behavior of various metrics. At this stage, three common measures of central tendency have been covered: the mean, the median, and the mode. More metrics to come!
The median is the 50th percentile, or 0.50 quantile (Chapter 25).
There is no convential notation for the median.

title: 25  Quantile
text:
Formal
Social media posts often feature puzzles claiming that solving them proves genius status or indicates that 99% of people cannot solve the problem. These claims are designed to suggest that solving the puzzle means an individual belongs to an exclusive, intellectual elite group.
While the specific percentages in these viral posts are usually fabricated to grab attention, an underlying statistical principle forms the basis of such claims.
Determining that 99% of people cannot solve a problem—or equivalently, that only 1% can—relies on relative position within a distribution. For instance: if 1,000 people attempt a problem and only 10 succeed, the success rate is 1%, placing those who solve it in the top 1%. Another approach implicitly links the puzzle-solving ability to a continuous quantitative ability (Chapter 17), such as IQ. Under this model, the top 1% corresponds to individuals whose IQ scores place them in the highest 1% of the distribution.
More generally, values can be ordered from smallest to largest to evaluate relative ranking. For any point in an ordered dataset, the proportion of values falling above or below that point can be calculated. A quantile identifies the specific value that splits a distribution into such given proportion. The median (Chapter 24) is a special case of quantile (0.5 quantile), where half of the observations fall below the value and half fall above.
The concept of a quantile generalizes the median. While the median splits a distribution into two equal halves (the 0.50 quantile), quantiles divide an ordered dataset or a probability distribution into arbitrary proportions \(p \in (0, 1)\).
Quantiles can be defined empirically using ordered data or using cumulative distribution.
In descriptive statistics, the \(p\)-quantile (often expressed as a percentile when multiplied by 100) is a value that separates the lowest fraction \(p\) of the ordered data from the remaining fraction \(1 - p\).
Consider a sample of \(n\) observations ordered in non-decreasing sequence:
\[x_{(1)} \le x_{(2)} \le \dots \le x_{(n)}\]
To locate the \(p\)-quantile, first determine the position index \(L_p\):
\[L_p = p(n + 1)\]
If \(L_p\) is an integer, the \(p\)-quantile corresponds directly to \(x_{(L_p)}\). If \(L_p\) is not an integer, linear interpolation is applied between the adjacent ordered values \(x_{(\lfloor L_p \rfloor)}\) and \(x_{(\lceil L_p \rceil)}\).
\[\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\]

title: 25  Quantile
text:
Quartiles are specific quantiles that divide an ordered dataset into four equal parts:

The first quartile (\(Q_1\), or 0.25 quantile) separates the lowest 25% of the data from the upper 75%.
The second quartile (\(Q_2\), or 0.50 quantile) corresponds to the sample median, dividing the dataset into two equal halves.
The third quartile (\(Q_3\), or 0.75 quantile) separates the lowest 75% of the data from the upper 25%.

The interquartile range (\(\text{IQR}\)) measures statistical dispersion by evaluating the spread of the middle 50% of the dataset. It is calculated as the difference between the third and first quartiles:

title: 25  Quantile
text:
Examples

Consider a dataset containing 100 observations formed by two distinct clusters: the integers from 1 to 50 and the integers from 1001 to 1050.
The \(1\%\), \(2\%\), and \(3\%\) quantiles (\(0.01\), \(0.02\), and \(0.03\) quantiles) correspond to 1, 2, and 3, respectively. Similarly, the \(20\%\) quantile is 20.
The median (\(0.50\) quantile) falls directly between the two clusters:
\[\text{Median} = \frac{50 + 1001}{2} = 525.5\]
The \(51\%\) quantile steps into the second cluster at 1001, while the \(98\%\) and \(99\%\) quantiles correspond to 1048 and 1049.
Visualizing quantiles within a distribution helps to illustrate how cutoffs map directly to specific proportions of data.

In a histogram (Chapter 19), a quantile represents the boundary value along the x-axis below which a specified percentage of total observations falls. For instance, the value corresponding to the 8% quantile divides the lowest 8% of the data (green region) from the upper 92%. Similarly, the 75% quantile—also known as the third quartile (Q3)—marks the boundary below which 75% of the observations lie.











The quantile can be easily inferred with a cumulative distribution (Chapter 20). (1) Pick the quantile percentage on the y-axis, (2)project a horizontal line (e.g., 8% or 75%) to where it intersects the cumulative curve, and then (3) drop a vertical line to the x-axis, which is the corresponding quantile value.

title: 25  Quantile
text:
Tips and warnings

The quantile is a pair: the proprtion \(p\) and the respective \(x\) value.
The interquartile range (\(\text{IQR}\)) measures the spread of the middle 50% of a distribution, calculated as the difference between the 75% and 25% quantiles (\(Q_3 - Q_1\)). The rectangles in a default boxplot represent the IQR and is a measure dispersion (alternative to the standard devitation).
Quantile estimates can become imprecise or unstable in small datasets. In such cases, linear interpolation or theoretical approximations may yield unreliable results.
A \(p\)-value of 0.06 is directly related to a 0.06 (0.94 or 0.03-0.97) quantile of the null distribution1. Using the IQ metaphor from the introduction, this corresponds to three possible interpretations: an IQ in the top 6%, in the bottom 6%, or split between the top 3% and bottom 3%. The first two interpretations describe one-sided statistics, whereas the last applies to a two-sided statistic.


Notation/Semantic/Terminology

Percentiles and quantiles describe identical statistical cutoffs. Mathematically, the \(p\)-quantile corresponds directly to the \((100 \times p)\)-th percentile. For example, the 0.50 quantile, the 50th percentile, and the median (\(Q_2\)) refer to the exact same value in a dataset.

title: Basic coding
text:
Traditionally, data analyses were conducted using software such as SPSS, Stata, and XLSTAT. However, the rise of R introduced a new paradigm for analyzing and visualizing data. Unlike those point-and-click tools, R is a programming language—and programming is a subject that is rarely included in traditional science curricula.
Learning a programming language like R often requires unlearning how computers are typically used. With touchscreens, mice, voice commands, and artificial intelligence (where human-computer interaction feels more like a standard conversation), typing commands directly into a keyboard can feel obsolete.
The Online Historical Encyclopaedia of Programming Languages (HOPL) records over 8,900 languages. Because most programming languages share the same core principles, understanding the basics makes transitioning between languages much easier. Although R is the only language used in this handbook, the general principles of programming are explained using R as a concrete example.
This section introduces the basic framework of computer programming, describing the console (26  Console), the script editor (27  Script editor), the Integrated Development Environment (28  IDE: Integrated Development Environment), and the concept of variable assignment (29  Variable assigment), and a function (40  Function).
It describes the elementary data types in programming: numbers (30  Type: Integer and numeric), strings or characters (32  Type: String or Character), and booleans (33  Type: Boolean), and the data structures built from these basic types to allow more flexible storage: vectors (35  Vector), matrices (36  Matrix), data frames (38  Data frame), and lists (39  List).
A series of chapters introduces the syntax to perform arithmetic (31  Arithmetic operation), matrix operations (37  Vector and matrix operation), and boolean operations (34  Boolean operation) in any programming languages.
Finally, two chapters cover two daily activities of a programmer: writing pseudocode (41  Pseudocode) and identifying and fixing bugs (42  Debugging).
Unlike previous sections, this section includes code snippets and their outputs. Code appears in light gray blocks, with the output displayed underneath in a distinct black font. Comments within the code start with a # symbol to explain what the lines do. Here is an example:

# The code below calculates 1 + 2
1 + 2

[1] 3


Practicing by copying, typing, and modifying these code examples is strongly recommended.

title: 26  Console
text:
Formal
Everyone knows how to use a calculator:
With most basic calculators, the display shows both the calculation (top line: this is a useful added feature to ensure the correct operation was entered) and the result on the bottom line Figure 26.1 (a).
A console functions exactly like the interface of a calculator Figure 26.1 (b):
Conceptually, the console is the interface that displays communication with the program. It shows the input and displays the output. This simple interface is common to many programs.
An R console is an interactive command-line interface that allows commands to be typed directly, executed immediately, and evaluated in real time. It operates on a continuous cycle known as a Read-Eval-Print Loop (REPL):

title: 26  Console
text:
Read: The console accepts code typed at the prompt.
Eval: The R engine evaluates and computes the code.
Print: The console displays the result, output, or error message.
Loop: A new prompt appears, waiting for the next command.

The console is just the display; the program that performs the actual calculation runs in the background.
A displayed prompt cannot be edited.
Typing directly into the console is not recommended; using a script editor (Chapter 27 and Chapter 28) is preferred.
Error message: This indicates that something is wrong with the code. It can be frustrating, but it is common (Chapter 42).

Command, code, and script are often used interchangeably to refer to the text typed for the program to evaluate.1
A prompt is the input indicator (e.g., >), although in the context of modern Artificial Intelligence, “prompt” also refers to the text instruction.
Run, evaluate, and execute can be used interchangeably.
Command-line interface (CLI), terminal, and console refer to the same concept in simple terms.2

title: 27  Script editor
text:
Formal
Those reading this handbook will almost certainly use R. This involves writing, copying, editing, and deleting line after line of code. For such an intensive task, making the experience as pleasant, productive, and efficient as possible is essential.
The core purpose of a script editor is to assist the user in every possible way. The most basic script editor available is a plain text editor (e.g., Notepad). It functions as a script editor because it allows text to be written, edited, and saved as code. In the early days of R, codes were written in Notepad or Notepad++ and then copied into the console (Chapter 26) for execution.
Today, many script editors exist, but most users rely on the editor included with an IDE (Chapter 28). Below are several key features that improve code writing:
Different script editors suit different needs (a personal assistant is choosen on specific skills needed to handle particular tasks). A programmer using multiple languages—such as Python, Java, and R—might prefer a multi-language editor. For the typical R user, the script editor built into RStudio is the most popular choice.
A script editor is a specialized text interface used by programmers to write, edit, and save code files. Unlike an interactive console (Chapter 26) that runs code immediately line-by-line, a script editor allows you to write out a full sequence of instructions, review them, and save them as a permanent file before running them.

title: 27  Script editor
text:
Examples

Code as it appears in the simplest text editor without syntax highlighting and indentation.
# Add one plus one
1 + 1

# Import your data into R
data <- read.csv('my_data.csv')

# A ggplot code
ggplot(data, aes(x = age, y = height)) +
geom_point()+
theme_bw()

The same code with syntax highlighting for different object types: comments in gray, numbers (Chapter 30) in red, functions (Chapter 40) in blue, and characters (Chapter 32) and variables (Chapter 29) in black.
# Add one plus one
1 + 1

# Import your data into R
data <- read.csv(“my_data.csv”)


# A ggplot code
ggplot(data, aes(x = age, y = height)) +
    geom_point()+
    theme_bw()
A script editor includes various features to facilitate coding and improve productivity. This figure (Figure 27.1) is an example the script editor in RStudio displaying syntax highlighting on lines 1,2 3, and syntax suggestion and auto-completion for log as well as the help file (yellow rectangle).






Figure 27.1: Features of script editor

title: 27  Script editor
text:
Tips and warnings

By definition, a script is meant for writing code. To evaluate code in the console, the brute-force approach is to copy the chunks run. However, code can be sent directly to the console while remaining in the script editor with an IDE (Chapter 28).
Documenting code: A good habit that is easy to ignore is adding human-readable text. While code is for the machine, other people and the original author can benefit from verbal descriptions. These are called comments (see the code preceded by # above). They are ignored during evaluation by the computer.
An underused feature of script editors is keyboard shortcuts. Exploring available shortcuts is a good habit. For example, using a shortcut for variable assignment <- is very useful when certain symbols are not easily accessible on the keyboard. Custom shortcuts can even be created.
Embracing the features: Most script editors are more powerful than expected. Exploring and learning features make coding more productive.
Code is written in plain text format. It can be opened with any text editor including Microsoft Word. However, features like syntax highlighting belong to the script editor, not the file itself (unlike a Word document with embedded bold formatting, etc.).
Because a code is stored in plain text files, it can easily be tracked using a version control program.
Themes allow personalization. Themes can be light or dark, with bright or muted colors. This can be customized in RStudio under Tools > Global Options > Appearance.


Notation/Semantic/Terminology

Command, code, and script are often used interchangeably to refer to the text typed for the program to evaluate.1

title: 28  IDE: Integrated Development Environment
text:
Formal
A common, innocent, and inconsequential mistake is to confuse R and RStudio. R is a programming language, whereas RStudio is a specialized IDE for R.
In the previous chapters, a console (Chapter 26) was presented as the minimal component needed to code—the interface between the human and the computer. As more is written, script editors assist the process of code writing (Chapter 27) (like having a personal assistant to assist with tasks). An IDE is the final stage of making coding more comfortable.
To use a metaphor: R is the car, a script editor is a set of accessories (steering wheel cover, leather seats, backup camera, etc.), and an IDE is a combination of an auto shop, a garage, and a co-pilot.
RStudio is the most popular IDE for R.
An IDE, or Integrated Development Environment, is a single software application that combines the essential tools needed to write, test, and debug code in one unified interface. Using RStudio as a main example, an IDE wraps around the basics:
Instead of writing code in a basic text editor, executing it in a separate terminal, and opening another window to view graphs, an IDE consolidates these workflow components under a single workspace.
