title: 29  Variable assigment
text:
Formal
sary_mainitirano.jpeg, foza orana.mp3, Malok'ila_1.mp4. Beyond clicking these files on a computer, consider how they actually work.
Suppose a filename is changed (renamed), for example: sary_maintirano.jpeg to sary_paris.jpeg. When opened, the image remains the photo taken in Maintirano. In other words, a filename is something symbolic—a label created by the user to indicate the content. It can be frustrating to find a file with no indication of its contents unless it is opened.
Fundamentally, file content is a sequence of 0s and 1s stored in the computer’s memory. To access this sequence, the address (the location of that sequence) is required. Figuratively, the filename is like the name of a house (e.g., Villa Fanomezana); the name can change, but the physical house and its address generally remain the same.
In programming, an assignment consists of binding three elements: creating an object (building a house) at a specific location (the address) and assigning it a chosen label. While one can choose what object to create and what to name it, the address itself (where it is placed in computer memory) is determined by the system—which is ultimately for the best.
In programming language design, assignment is defined as a mechanism that dynamically changes the binding between a storage location and a value. It introduces the foundational concepts of L-values (location/address) and R-values (read/data value).
In R, the syntax is: variablename <- object which reads: put the object in memory and assign it a name. The assignment operator essentially creates a new variable name, allocates an address, and stores the created object there.
An object can be almost anything; in fact, the rest of this section covers the different types of fundamental objects, from Chapter 30 to Chapter 39.

title: 29  Variable assigment
text:
Examples

Assignment and console output

# Store the number(object) 2 in variable called a.
a <- 2

In the first example above, the number (object/value) 2 is stored in a variable called a. Running that line in R produces no output in the console, because the instruction is to create the object, not to evaluate it.

# this will display the value stored in a
a

[1] 2


Adding numbers two numbers using their names: Instead of calculating 2 + 3 directly, 2 can be stored in a and 3 in b. Then, a + b can be added and stored in c. Notice that variable names are symbolic.

# Creating two variables to store the value 2 and 3
a <- 2

b <- 3

# Storing the result of the calculation
c <- a + b

# Display the value in c
c

[1] 5


Swapping values: A very instructive exercise for understanding assignment is swapping the contents of two variables.

# Defining the two variables
variable1 <- 1
variable2 <- 20

# Swapping elements between box
# Put the value of variable1 to variable2
variable2 <- variable1
# Put the value of variable2 to variable1
variable1 <- variable2


# Print the value of variable1
variable1

[1] 1

# Print the value of variable2
variable2

[1] 1


It does not work!!! the value inside variable1 becomes 1 (no swap occurs), and variable2 also becomes 1. The solution to this exercies is similar to swapping juice in a cup and coffee in a glass: to swap the contents, one must first transfer one of the beverages into a third container before proceeding.

# Creating two variables
variable1 <- 1
variable2 <- 20

# Swapping elements using a thrid temproray variable
temporary <- variable1
variable1 <- variable2
variable2 <- temporary


# Print the values in variable1

variable1

[1] 20

# Print the values in variable2
variable2

[1] 1


The values are swapped.

title: 29  Variable assigment
text:
Tips and warnings

The default shortcut for <- in RStudio on Windows is Alt + - and Option + - on Mac.
The three variables below are all different. Object names are case sensitive and typo sensitive.

my_variable <- 2,
my_Variable <- 2,
my_varable <- 2

The most common error in programming is shown below Figure 29.1. While it can cause panic, it is the easiest to solve, and the main culprits are:

Typos: case sensitivity, spelling etc.
Unassigned variables, where code was typed in the script but not executed, so the object is not stored in the environment







Figure 29.1: Object not found



In R, = can also be used for object assignment (a = 2 works as well). However, <- is preferred, reserving = for specific contexts such as passing arguments inside functions.
The rightward assignment operator -> is also supported (2 -> a).
Creating evocative variable names is a good habit so the content can easily be inferred.
Variable naming conventions:

No spaces or special characters (%, $, etc.)
Cannot start with a number or an underscore
Multi-word conventions:

TelmaNumber and MadacomNumber (PascalCase)
telmaNumber and madacomNumber (camelCase)
telma_number and madacom_number (snake_case)
TELMA_NUMBER and MADACOM_NUMBER (screaming snake_case)
telma.number and madacom.number (informal dot.case)


After evaluation, the top-right panel shows all created objects, along with their names and values.







Figure 29.2: All the variables that was evaluated in the console appear on the right with their values




Notation/Semantic/Terminology
The word variable has now appeared in mathematics, statistics (Chapter 16), and in R. Does it mean the same thing? Fundamentally, yes. It is a combination of notation (variable name) and a value. A variable is symbolic in mathematics (think of \(x\), \(f(x)\), or \(y\)) because it is understood that it could take any value, it varies. In statistics, a variable also takes different values for different individuals in the population, although the variable is often thought of as the realized values and thus a sequence of values. The variable in programming embraces two perspectives: (1) it can be symbolic as in mathematics (which is why many examples will use names like \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), etc.) to store a value that could be replaced at any time, and (2) it stores the sequences of characteristics of a population as vectors (Chapter 35) and data frames (Chapter 38) that, once recorded, will not change. Variable names becomes height or age. There are more nuances if one digs deeper into a more rigorous definition, but intuitively, this distinction suffices.

title: 30  Type: Integer and numeric
text:
Formal
The primary function of a program is to perform calculations. The most obvious objects that can be created, stored, and manipulated are numbers. There are two types of numbers, following the concepts in mathematics (Chapter 3) and in statistics (Chapter 17).
A whole number (discrete variables) are represented by integers and are used for counting and indexing. In R programming, real numbers (continuous variables) are called numeric.
While knowing these distinctions is important, R is generally very flexible regarding the two types. It handles conversions automatically without failing or issuing errors if a numeric is used where an integer is expected. For instance, attempting to use the numeric 2.3 instead of the integer 2 to specify the length of a vector (Chapter 35) are handled internally.1

title: 30  Type: Integer and numeric
text:
Assigning an integer value to a variable: to force R to interpret a number as an integer, append L after the number.

# Storing the integer 24 in the variable my_favorite_integer
my_favorite_integer <- 24L

Assigning a numeric value to a variable: numeric generally refers to numbers with decimals. The decimal separator in programming languages is a period .. A comma , is used as a list separator (see Chapter 35, Chapter 36, and Chapter 39).

# Storing the number 24.022
a_real_number <- 24.022

If L is not specified, R automatically assumes that the value is numeric.

my_fake_integer <- 24

title: 30  Type: Integer and numeric
text:
Examples

# Built-in constants (such as pi) are natively available in R
pi

[1] 3.141593

# Mathematical functions like sqrt() evaluate to numeric values
sqrt(2)

[1] 1.414214

# Assign a numeric  value to a variable
my_number <- 2.13

# The 'L' suffix forces R to store the value explicitly as an integer
a <- 2L

# Without the 'L' suffix, whole numbers default to numeric
cc <- 2

# str() inspects the internal structure of an object; here it confirms 'a' is an integer
str(a)

 int 2

# str() confirms 'cc' is a numeric
str(cc)

 num 2


The type of object is shown on the left, above int for integer and num for numeric.

title: 30  Type: Integer and numeric
text:
Tips and warnings

An integer requires less computer memory. However, memory is usually not an issue, and memory management is beyond the scope of this handbook.
As a shortcut, the leading zero before a decimal point can be omitted:

# .123 is the same as 0.123
a <- .123

Machine vs. mathematics: there are limits on the number of decimals and the maximum value a computer can store and compute.

# The largest integer
.Machine$integer.max

[1] 2147483647

# The largest postive numeric
.Machine$double.xmax

[1] 1.797693e+308

# The smallest value (machine precision)
.Machine$double.eps

[1] 2.220446e-16


Astronomically large numbers are not supported and are rarely required in typical ecological workflows.
Due to precision limitations, multiplying very small numbers by very large numbers can lead to numerical instability and should be avoided.
Infinity is not a finite number and is represented by Inf and -Inf

title: 30  Type: Integer and numeric
text: The drawback is that one must either trust R to manage the mistake or understand how it handles implicit coercion to use it efficiently.↩︎

title: 31  Arithmetic operation
text:
Formal
R is primarily a calculator, and the purpose of this chapter is to show the sytnax for basic arithmetic operations—as taught since primary school—into their R equivalents. These operations are identical across programming languages, so this is not specific to R. Operations follow the standard order of operations (Chapter 1), so attention to precedence is required.

title: 31  Arithmetic operation
text:
Addition: symbol + as in a + b
Subtraction: symbol - as in a - b
Multiplication: symbol * as in a * b. Here it is worth noting that this differs from \(a \times b, \; a b, \; \text{and } a.b\), which are mathematical notations, not programming syntax.
Division: symbol / as in a / b. This is also different from \(a \div b\) and \(\frac{a}{b}\), which are mathematical notations rather than programming syntax.
Power: symbol ^ as in a^b.
Parentheses: symbol () as in (a + b)^2. Be careful, as () is also used for functions (Chapter 40). Additionally, {} and [] are not substitutes for parentheses.1

title: 31  Arithmetic operation
text:
Examples

# Addition: computes the sum of 1 and 1
1 + 1

[1] 2

# Negation: evaluates 2 minus 11
2 - 11

[1] -9

# Multiplication: calculates 2 times 1
2 * 1

[1] 2

# Division: computes the quotient of 1 divided by 2
1 / 2

[1] 0.5

# Exponentiation (power): raises 2 to the power of 6
2^6

[1] 64

# Grouping with parentheses: forces (1 + 1) to evaluate first before multiplying by 3
(1 + 1) * 3

[1] 6

title: 31  Arithmetic operation
text:
Tips and warnings

Here is a list of common mistakes that will display an error message:
Multiplication is often omitted. For example, \(2\pi\) in mathematics is not written as 2 pi in R. Multiplication must be explicit, so the equivalent is 2 * pi. The same rule applies to (a + b) * c.
Parentheses come in pairs, and closing parentheses are sometimes forgotten. However, using a good script editor automatically adds the closing parenthesis.
Leaving spaces around expressions improves readability (e.g., a * b instead of a*b).
The modulo (remainder) is implemented using 5 %% 3.
These arithmetic symbols have special meanings in R, which is why they cannot be used when naming a variable.

title: 31  Arithmetic operation
text: Curly brackets are used to group multiple statements into a single code block, and square brackets for indexing and subsetting vectors, matrices, data frames, and lists ↩︎

title: 32  Type: String or Character
text:
Formal
The first exercise in programming is printing text to the console. While this is trivial in languages like R, printing text in languages such as Fortran, C, or C++ can feel like an odyssey for an absolute beginner. When one finally manages to understand the computer’s logic, figuratively taming and bringing the machine into the world of the living, the very first order is to ask it to greet: “Hello world”.
A computer program is more than a basic calculator, which should be clear by now. A major feature of a computer program is its ability to handle non-numeric data. Such objects are called strings, which is why printing “Hello world” involves string manipulation.
Unlike numbers, arithmetic operations cannot be performed on strings—letters or words cannot be multiplied or divided. Manipulating strings requires non-mathematical operations that are natural to human language, such as deleting a letter or word, combining text, or replacing text.
For most ecological applications and the purpose of this handbook, strings represent qualitative variables (Chapter 18). For example, entries such as “male” or “female” are treated as strings, in contrast to numeric measurements like height or weight.
A string or character vector is an object type used to represent text, defined by enclosing content within quotation marks ("" or '').
# Print a string directly to the console
"This is a string or character"

[1] "This is a string or character"
When a string is displayed in the console, R includes quotation marks to indicate its character data type.
# Inspect the structure of a character scalar
str("a")

 chr "a"
The character type is abbreviated as chr in structure outputs generated by str().

title: 32  Type: String or Character
text:
Examples
Assigning a character to a variable

# A character object containing a single letter
one_letter <- "R"

# A character object containing a single word
a_word <- "Hello"

# A character object containing a sentence
long_string <- "Ny akoho tsy nanidina tsy nahandry ny andro zoma."

title: 32  Type: String or Character
text:
Tips and warnings

Any special character can be included inside a string

"There is no problem in usin$ spécial character in a string, & < is not ! or 1 2 3"

[1] "There is no problem in usin$ spécial character in a string, & < is not ! or 1 2 3"


Performing arithmetic operations on string objects produces an error because mathematical operators are not defined for character data:

# Defined as a character string, not a numeric value
string_1 <- "1"

# Defined as a character string, not a numeric value
string_2 <- "2026"

#Attempting addition on character strings triggers an error
string_1 + string_2

Error in string_1 + string_2: non-numeric argument to binary operator


"Magadascar" is a specific sequence of letters and differs from "Madagascar", just as 12 differs from 21. While order differences in numbers are easily spotted, typographical errors in text are harder to detect. Typos are unavoidable.
Lingering spaces: entering data in spreadsheet software like MS Excel or graphical interfaces frequently introduces subtle errors. Beyond capitalization typos (e.g., "male" vs. "Male"), a hidden typo that remains unnoticed in spreadsheet software is a trailing space like "male ". Data cleaning is therefore necessary when importing datasets into R1.
Distinguishing between three distinct concepts that share the same name

# A string literal composed of three characters
"sin"

[1] "sin"

# A  variable named sin storing a character string
sin <- "sin"

# A variable named siin storing the value 2
siin <- 2

# The trigonometric sine function, identified by trailing parentheses () computing the sine of the variable siin
sin(siin)

[1] 0.9092974


Combine strings using the function paste() and specify a delimiter using the sep argument, such as an empty string "", a comma ",", a comma followed by a space ", ", or any arbitrary character sequence:

# Combine strings with no separation
paste("Hello", "world", sep = "")

[1] "Helloworld"

# Combine strings with a comma separator
paste("Hello", "world", sep = ",")

[1] "Hello,world"

# Combine strings with a comma and space separator
paste("Hello", "world", sep = ", ")

[1] "Hello, world"

# Combine strings using a custom text delimiter
paste("Hello", "world", sep = " anything you want ")

[1] "Hello anything you want world"


The paste() function accepts multiple string arguments and works with variable names in place of raw string values:

# Combine three strings with a custom separator
paste("Hello", "world", "life", sep = " there ")

[1] "Hello there world there life"

# Assign string values to variables
word1 <- "Hello"
word2 <- "world"

# Combine variables; default separator is a single space " "
paste(word1, word2, word1, word2)

[1] "Hello world Hello world"




Notation/Semantic/Terminology

String is the universal term in programming, whereas character is the standard term used in R. A third object type, called a factor, also exists in R.2
In R, double quotation marks "" and single quotation marks '' can be used interchangeably. Some R practitioners prefer single quotes, whereas multi-language programmers often prefer "" to maintain consistent syntax across languages.

title: 32  Type: String or Character
text:
covered in a subsequent volume↩︎
Factors are better illustrated later alongside vectors (Chapter 35).↩︎

title: 33  Type: Boolean
text:
Formal
The chapter (Chapter 31) provide the syntax to perform arithmetic operation Chapter 1. For instance the multiplication is encoded as asterisk *. Notable symbols that have not yet been used include inequality operators (<, >, >=, <=) and the equality operator (=).
What does it mean to write 2 < 3, or 2 > 3? The first expression is a correct statement (true), while the other is incorrect (false). This concept applies directly to programming: these symbols serve as comparisons between the left-hand and right-hand side. A Boolean variable is a specialized object type that stores the result of such comparisons as either true or false.
In data-science, Boolean objects can encode qualitative variables (Chapter 18) when there are two outcomes: dead or alive, present or absent, or true or false. While strings or numeric types can also store binary data, Booleans are more explicit because they are restricted to exactly two values.
A Boolean variable type represents binary truth values used to evaluate logical conditions and control program flow.
To make it explicit, Booleans are specifically represented by TRUE or FALSE in R (T and F are also shorthand alternatives).
# str() inspects the internal structure of an object
str(TRUE)

 logi TRUE

title: 33  Type: Boolean
text:
Syntax for relational operations:

To evaluate if a is strictly smaller to b, the expression is a < b.
To evaluate if a is smaller than or equal to b the expression is a <= b;
To evaluate if a is strictly larger to b the expression: a > b.
To evaluate if a is larger than or equal to b the expression is a >= b;

Syntax for testing equality: because = is used for variable assignment and in function arguments (Chapter 40), the convention is to use double equal signs ==. Thus, the expression to evalute whether a is equal to b is written as a == b^.
Syntax for testing inequality: to evaluate whether a is different from b, the expression is written as a != b.
In R, the boolean type is encoded as logi, short for logical

title: 33  Type: Boolean
text:
Examples

# Define variables
var1 <- 3^2
var2 <- 2^3

# Test for equality (returns FALSE)
var1 == var2

[1] FALSE

# Test for inequality (returns TRUE)
var1 != var2

[1] TRUE

# Evaluate if var1 is strictly smaller than var2 (returns FALSE)
var1 < var2

[1] FALSE

# Evaluate if var1 is greater than or equal to 1 (returns TRUE)
var1 >= 1

[1] TRUE

title: 33  Type: Boolean
text:
Tips and warnings

These symbols have the same meaning (as those in arithmetic operatio Chapter 31) are the same in most programming languages.
While it is convenient to encode data as dead or alive or other symbol (maty and velona) during data entry (Chapter 38). Converting them to boolean TRUE and FALSE is generally done during the data cleaning phase.
It is better to use TRUE and FALSE when encoding boolean variable. While T and F are shorthand, they could be mixed with variable name. In contrast, the syntax TRUE and FALSE are protected and thus cannot be used otherwise.
NA is a third special protect to mean empty.
In R, it is possible to perform arithmetic operation on boolean variable. The operation below works because R coerce them as 0 and 1 and thus proceed forward with the calculation.

# Assign Boolean values (FALSE implicitly equals 0, TRUE implicitly equals 1)
a <- FALSE
b <- TRUE

# Arithmetic operations automatically coerce Booleans to numbers (0 + 1 = 1)
a + b

[1] 1

# Multiplication with a zero value yields zero (0 * 1 = 0)
a * b

[1] 0

# Subtraction of numeric representations (0 - 1 = -1)
a - b

[1] -1

# Division of zero by one (0 / 1 = 0)
a / b

[1] 0




Notation/Semantic/Terminology
Boolean originates from mathematical logic (Boolean algebra). Binary refers specifically to systems with two possible states, while logical indicates values evaluated as true or false.

title: 34  Boolean operation
text:
Formal
The title above is a joke between two logicians1. However, normal people never find it funny!
Operations with numbers are intuitive (Chapter 1), whereas operations on logical or Boolean variables (Chapter 33) are less intuitive. Consider the Boolean variables (also called statements or propositions) below:
A: Radama is male – TRUE
B: Radama is Malagasy – TRUE
C: Ranavalona is male – FALSE
D: Ranavalona is Malagasy – TRUE
Boolean operations combine propositions using logical operators:
P1: A AND B: Radama is male AND Radama is Malagasy.
P1 evaluates to TRUE. Formally: TRUE AND TRUE = TRUE.
P2: A OR B: Radama is male OR Radama is Malagasy.
P2 evaluates to TRUE. Formally: TRUE OR TRUE = TRUE.
P3: C AND D: Ranavalona is male AND Ranavalona is Malagasy.
P3 evaluates to FALSE. Formally: FALSE AND TRUE = FALSE.
P4: C OR D: Ranavalona is male OR Ranavalona is Malagasy.
P4 evaluates to TRUE. Formally: FALSE OR TRUE = TRUE.
Returning to the joke, the question can be reframed as two propositions:
Proposition 1: The newborn is male.
Proposition 2: The newborn is female.
Proposition 1 OR Proposition 2 evaluates to TRUE because one statement must be true.
Boolean operations form a fundamental part of programming and can feel unintuitive to non-logicians. Acquiring basic proficiency in logic is essential. Concrete applications are illustrated in the tips section below.
The AND operator is encoded as & in R (A & B or A && B).
The OR operator is encoded as | in R (A | B or A || B).
The single operators (&, |) perform element-wise evaluation, which serves as the primary method for vector filtering in data analysis.
The double operators (&&, ||) perform short-circuit evaluation, typically used in conditional statements and loops. These are rarely used in this handbook except in specific advanced scenarios.
A final symbol is !, which is used for negation. The expression !A evaluates to the logical opposite of A.

title: 34  Boolean operation
text:
Examples

#| echo: true

# Assign Boolean values to variables
a <- TRUE
b <- TRUE
cc <- FALSE

# Logical OR: returns TRUE if at least one side is TRUE
a | b

[1] TRUE

# Logical AND: returns TRUE only if both sides are TRUE
a & b

[1] TRUE

# Logical AND with a FALSE value: evaluates to FALSE
a & cc

[1] FALSE

# Combined logical operation (AND has higher precedence than OR)
a | (b & cc)

[1] TRUE

# Grouped logical operation: parentheses force evaluation of (a | b) first
(a | b) & cc

[1] FALSE

# Negation: flips TRUE to FALSE (and vice versa)
!a

[1] FALSE

title: 34  Boolean operation
text:
Tips and warnings

Although the concept of data frame is needed to full understand the example below. The example below combines and uses variable types, relational operators, and Boolean operators to filter individuals matching combined criteria:
nationality == "Malagasy" & (male == TRUE | height < 1.6)
In this expression, nationality, male, and height are variable names (Chapter 29) of type character (Chapter 32), logical (Chapter 33), and numeric (Chapter 30), respectively. The relational operators == and < filter within variables, whereas the Boolean operators & and | evaluate conditions across variables.
These Boolean operators correspond to the concepts of intersection (AND) and union (OR) in set theory. For example, in nationality == "Malagasy" & male == TRUE the operation essentialy intersect the set of malagasy and male.
Performing Boolean operations are prone to mistakes because logical evaluation can be surprisingly counterintuitive. Extra caution is required during implementation.

title: 34  Boolean operation
text: mathematicians who specialize in the study of logic↩︎

title: 35  Vector
text:
Formal
Historically, populations resided in rural hamlets, but spatial limits eventually forced housing to expand vertically. The implication is that instead of having an address for ten separate homes (recycling the metaphor from variable assignment Chapter 29), there is now one address for the building along with a floor number.
A vector in programming is essentially a higher-level object that stores a sequence of the same type. To access any specific value, one only needs to know the name of the building and the floor number.
This analogy only holds in progamming when each floor—called an element—is of the same type (all numbers, all logical values, or all strings). If the elements are heterogeneous, a list is used instead (Chapter 39). Vector indexing relies on integers (Chapter 3).
The key point is that a vector is a new type of object constructed from a sequence of elementary types. It shares a similar structure to basic variables: variable name, assignment operator, and value–which is a now sequence. Values can be retrieved based on their order in the sequence. In practice, vectors are used to store data corresponding to a single variable (Chapter 16).
To construct a vector in R, the syntax c() —short for concatenate—is used.

title: 35  Vector
text:
vector_name <- c(object1, object2, ..., objectn)

The length of a vector is the number of elements it contains and can be retrieved with length().
To access the \(p^{th}\) element of a vector, square brackets [] are used. In the example above, vector_name[2] returns object2. The positional order is called the index and must be an integer.
In R, a negative index excludes the element. For example, vector_name[-2] removes object2 from the output.

title: 35  Vector
text:
Examples

Constructing vectors.

# Creating a Boolean vector
c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE)

[1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE

# Creating an integer vector
c(2L, 1L, 4L)

[1] 2 1 4

# Creating a character vector
c("Hello", "world", "Goodbye")

[1] "Hello"   "world"   "Goodbye"

# Assigning a vector to a variable
my_vector <- c("Hello", "world", "Goodbye")

Accessing single values.

# Outputting the first element
my_vector[1]

[1] "Hello"

# Outputting the second element
my_vector[2]

[1] "world"


Accessing multiple values by subsetting with a vector of indices.

# Outputting the first and second elements
my_vector[c(1, 2)]

[1] "Hello" "world"

# Outputting the second and first elements in reverse order
my_vector[c(2, 1)]

[1] "world" "Hello"

# Storing the indices as a vector
vector_index <- c(2, 3)
my_vector[vector_index]

[1] "world"   "Goodbye"


Constructing vectors from existing vectors.

vec1 <- c(1, 4, 5)
vec2 <- c(10, 11, 12)

# Combine the two vectors
vec_combined <- c(vec1, vec2)

# Append a single value to the existing vector
vec_combined <- c(vec_combined, 123)

Deleting one or more elements.

# Remove the first element
vec_combined[-1]

[1]   4   5  10  11  12 123

# Remove the first and fourth elements
vec_combined[c(-1, -4)]

[1]   4   5  11  12 123


Notice that these operations do not modify the stored variable; they return and display the subsetted vector.

# Extract and store in a new variable
sub_vector <- vec_combined[c(-1, -4)]
sub_vector

[1]   4   5  11  12 123


One can overwrite the original variable by reassigning the subsetted result, but note that the previous values cannot be recovered once overwritten.

# Overwrite the variable with the subsetted result
vec_combined <- vec_combined[c(-1, -4)]
vec_combined

[1]   4   5  11  12 123

title: 35  Vector
text:
Tips and warnings

A vector of length n can be seen as a n-dimensional object.
All elements in a vector must be of the same type. If different data types are combined, R automatically converts—or coerces—the values according to a strict hierarchy: Logical < Integer < Numeric < Character. Values lower in this hierarchy are converted to the higher type. The function structure is used to assess the type of vector.

Booleans to Integer


# Boolean values are coerced to Integer (TRUE becomes 1L, FALSE becomes 0L)
str(c(TRUE, FALSE, 4L))

 int [1:3] 1 0 4



Integer to Numeric


# Boolean values are coerced to Numeric (TRUE becomes 1, FALSE becomes 0)
str(c(TRUE, FALSE, 4))

 num [1:3] 1 0 4

# Integers are coerced to Numeric (1L and 2L become numeric 1 and 2)
str(c(1L, 2L, 4))

 num [1:3] 1 2 4


Numeric to Character

# Boolean values are coerced to Character (TRUE becomes "TRUE")
str(c(TRUE, TRUE, "text"))

 chr [1:3] "TRUE" "TRUE" "text"

# Both Boolean and Numeric values are coerced to Character (TRUE becomes "TRUE", 1.2 becomes "1.2")
str(c(TRUE, 1.2, "text"))

 chr [1:3] "TRUE" "1.2" "text"


This coercion can cause issues when importing data into R. If a column is supposed to be a numeric vector, but a single element cannot be parsed as numeric (e.g., the letter O instead of the number 0), R will convert all elements to character.
When printing long vectors in R, the bracketed numbers shown at the beginning of each line—such as [1], [38], or [75]—indicate the index of the first element displayed on that specific line. Because output wraps according to the width of the console window, these index markers dynamically adjust to help track element positions across multiple lines.



  [1]  3  4  2  4  3  2  2  6  8  3  6  6  4  4  3  5  2  2  1  2  4  6  3  4  3
 [26]  4  5  3  4  5  2  3  3  5 10  5  3  5  4  3  4  0  4  4  7  2  3  2  3  6
 [51]  2  1  4  2  3  6  4  3  4  7  4  6  0  3  5  1  5  1  7  2  3  3  3  5  5
 [76]  5  6  7  5  2  6  3  8  4  1  6  2  4  3  4  2  4  3  3  6  1  4  4  8  3



The elementary object (Chapter 30, Chapter 32, Chapter 33) are all considered as vector in R. The [1] means R displays the first element

# 1 is a numeric vector of length 1
1

[1] 1

# Hello is a character vector of length 1
"Hello"

[1] "Hello"

# TRUE is a logical vector of length 1
TRUE

[1] TRUE


In R, using a numeric index—such as vector_name[1.2]—behaves identically to vector_name[1]. By design, R automatically truncates the decimal portion (rounding down toward zero) to reduce the value to an integer index. While this index behavior can be convenient, it can also mask unintended non-integer values during indexing operations.
Elements within a vector can also be accessed by name rather than position. This approach is useful for short vectors or specialized operations where named elements make code clearer and eliminate the need to track index positions. Assigning labels creates a named vector by attaching a names attribute to the underlying elements.

# Create a named numeric vector representing room dimensions
room <- c(width = 15, height = 12)

# Display the attributes attached to the vector
attributes(room)

$names
[1] "width"  "height"

# Access an element by its assigned name instead of an index position
room["width"]

width 
   15 


Notice that when creating a named vector, element names are assigned using unquoted syntax similar to variable assignment (e.g., width = 15), but when subsetting by name, the name must be provided as a character string (e.g., room[“width”])

In R, a factor in R is a data structure used to store character vector. It stores character values as vector of integer codes mapped to a fixed set of predefined character labels called levels. It is memory efficient and also support ordering the values


# Constructing a character vector
my_vector <- c("a", "c", "a", "b")

# Transforming a vector to a factor
my_factor <- as.factor(my_vector)

# The ouptput is the same expect the addition of levels
my_factor

[1] a c a b
Levels: a b c

# But the structure of a factor is different
str(my_factor)

 Factor w/ 3 levels "a","b","c": 1 3 1 2


Each level corresponds to an integer: a to 1, b to 2 and c to 3. The sequence 1 3 1 2 is then reconstructed from that mapping. This is memory efficient because instead of storing a sequence of “characters” which takes more memory than a sequence of integer.

# Constructing an ordered factor
my_factor_ordered <- factor(
  my_vector,
  levels  = c("b", "a", "c"),
  ordered = TRUE)

# Printing the value
my_factor_ordered

[1] a c a b
Levels: b < a < c

# Examining the structure
str(my_factor_ordered)

 Ord.factor w/ 3 levels "b"<"a"<"c": 2 3 2 1


Ordering is pointless in the example but could be useful for ordinal such as age class or altitudinal class.

title: 36  Matrix
text:
Formal
A matrix is a programming implementation of a mathematical matrix Chapter 5. It is a rectangular object where each element is identified by its row and column position.
Reusing the analogy of a vector as a stacked apartment building Chapter 35, a matrix allows multiple apartments on each floor. An apartment is then identified by its floor number and its position on that floor. Similar to a vector, a matrix must be homogeneous. A matrix can therefore be described by its data type, such as an integer matrix or a numeric matrix.
In data science, datasets are often heterogeneous, in which case a data frame Chapter 38 or a list Chapter 39 is used. In general, a matrix object is best suited for mathematical computation.
To construct a matrix in R, the syntax matrix() is used.
The data argument takes a vector of length n_rows * n_cols so that each value is assigned to all the entry of the matrix. By default, R fills matrices column-by-column.

title: 36  Matrix
text:
matrix_name <- matrix(data, nrow = n_rows, ncol = n_cols)


The dimensions of a matrix represent the number of rows and columns it contains and can be retrieved with dim(). Alternatively, nrow() and ncol() return the row and column counts individually.
To access an element in a matrix, square brackets with a comma [row, column] are used: matrix_name[2, 3] returns the entry at the second row and third column. The positional indices must be integers.
In R, negative indices exclude specific rows or columns. For example, matrix_name[-2, ] excludes the second row, while matrix_name[, -3] excludes the third column from the output.

title: 36  Matrix
text:
Examples
Constructing the matrix used in Chapter 5.

mat <-
    matrix(c(6, 3, 0, 1, 3, 1, 10, 0, 0.5, 0, 0, 2),
    nrow = 4,
    ncol = 3)
mat

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    6    3  0.5
[2,]    3    1  0.0
[3,]    0   10  0.0
[4,]    1    0  2.0


Notice that numerical values are automatically formatted in the console output. When a matrix or vector contains at least one decimal number, R displays all numeric values in that structure with consistent decimal formatting (e.g., 6.0 or 3.0) to preserve alignment across rows and columns.

# Access the entire first row by specifying row index 1 and leaving the column index blank
mat[1, ]

[1] 6.0 3.0 0.5

# Access the entire first column by specifying column index 1 and leaving the row index blank
mat[, 1]

[1] 6 3 0 1

# Access the entry at row 3, column 2
mat[3, 2]

[1] 10

# Access elements in columns 1 and 2 of the first row
mat[1, c(1, 2)]

[1] 6 3

# Access rows 2 and 4 across all columns
mat[c(2, 4), ]

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    3    1    0
[2,]    1    0    2

# Access columns 1 and 3 across all rows
mat[, c(1, 3)]

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    6  0.5
[2,]    3  0.0
[3,]    0  0.0
[4,]    1  2.0

title: 36  Matrix
text:
Tips and warnings

The indexing [row_index, column_index] follows the \(a_{i,j}\) notation used in mathematics to denote the entry at row \(i\) and column \(j\) Chapter 5. Leaving one of the dimension blank means seleection all values along that dimension.
A matrix is typically used for mathematical operations Chapter 6 and Chapter 7.
Notice that there is no separate chapter on vectors in basic mathematics. This is because, mathematically, a vector is a matrix where either the number of rows or the number of columns is equal to one.
All elements in a matrix must be of the same data type. If different data types are combined, R automatically converts—or coerces—the entire matrix according to a strict hierarchy: Logical < Integer < Numeric < Character. Values lower in this hierarchy are converted to the higher type across all entries. See examples of coercion in Chapter 35.
Column and row names can also be assigned to a matrix. However, this is not the most common use of a matrix; a data frame Chapter 38 is more commonly used for named tabular data.

# Assign names to rows
rownames(mat) <- c("Rabe", "Rakoto", "Sanda", "Dora")

# Assign names to columns
colnames(mat) <- c("Banana", "Strawberries", "Voatsinefy")

# Display matrix with dimnames
mat

       Banana Strawberries Voatsinefy
Rabe        6            3        0.5
Rakoto      3            1        0.0
Sanda       0           10        0.0
Dora        1            0        2.0

title: 37  Vector and matrix operation
text:
Formal
The sole purpose of this chapter is to introduce the symbols and syntax for matrix operations (element-wise arithmetic operations and matrix algebra operations) in R. This implements the mathematical concepts presented in Chapter 6 and Chapter 7.

title: 37  Vector and matrix operation
text:
Scalar operation: when combining a number and a vector or a matrix, the same symbol notation addition +, subtraction -, multiplication *, division /.This is the same as in Chapter 6.

  2 * c(a, b) = c(2 * a, 2 * b)

Element-wise operation: when two objects are the same dimensions (vector of same length or matrix of same dimensions), the same symbols are used.
c(a, b) * c(c, d) = c(a * c, b * d)
Matrix multiplication (as in Chapter 7): the R implementation symbol is %*%. The star is to remember that it is still a multiplication. Unlike the arithmetic operation which is the same in any langauge, this syntax is specific to R.

title: 37  Vector and matrix operation
text:
Examples

Scalar operations

# Define a numeric vector of length 3
vec <- c(2, 0, 1)

# Multiply each element in the vector by a scalar (-2)
-2 * vec

[1] -4  0 -2

# Divide a scalar (10) by each vector element; division by zero yields Inf
10 / vec

[1]   5 Inf  10

# Divide each element in the vector by a scalar (10)
vec / 10

[1] 0.2 0.0 0.1

# Create a 2x3 matrix using vector values
mat <- matrix(c(2, 3, 4, vec), nrow = 2)

# Multiply all entries in the matrix by a scalar (-2)
-2 * mat

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]   -4   -8    0
[2,]   -6   -4   -2


Element-wise operations between vectors of equal length

# Define a second numeric vector of equal length (3)
new_vec <- c(10, 20, 30)

# Add corresponding elements of the two vectors
vec + new_vec

[1] 12 20 31

# Multiply corresponding elements of the two vectors
vec * new_vec

[1] 20  0 30


Matrix multiplication to calculate total expenditure per person per shop Chapter 7

# Define a 4x3 matrix representing quantities of fruits purchased
fruit_quantity <- matrix(
  data = c(6, 3, 0, 1, 3, 1, 10, 0, 0.5, 0, 0, 2),
  nrow = 4,
  ncol = 3
)

# Display the fruit quantity matrix
fruit_quantity

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    6    3  0.5
[2,]    3    1  0.0
[3,]    0   10  0.0
[4,]    1    0  2.0

# Define a 3x2 matrix representing fruit prices at two different shops
price_shops <- matrix(
  data = c(500, 1000, 2000, 600, 800, 2500),
  nrow = 3
)

# Display the price matrix
price_shops

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]  500  600
[2,] 1000  800
[3,] 2000 2500

# Perform matrix multiplication (%*%) to compute total expenditure per person per shop
fruit_quantity %*% price_shops

      [,1] [,2]
[1,]  7000 7250
[2,]  2500 2600
[3,] 10000 8000
[4,]  4500 5600

title: 37  Vector and matrix operation
text:
Tips and warnings

A diagonal matrix (where all elements outside the main diagonal are zero) can be created using diag(vec), where vec specifies the values along the diagonal. A useful shortcut is diag(m); when given a single integer m, it creates an identity matrix with ones along the main diagonal

# A 2 x 2 diagonal matrix
diag(c(12, 37))

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]   12    0
[2,]    0   37

# A 4 x 4 identity matrix
diag(4)

     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
[1,]    1    0    0    0
[2,]    0    1    0    0
[3,]    0    0    1    0
[4,]    0    0    0    1


The standard mathematical order of operations, parentheses, and rules apply. In matrix multiplication, the number of columns in the first matrix must equal the number of rows in the second matrix, and matrix division is undefined Chapter 7.
R is vectorized, meaning that when the argument is a vector, a function operates on each element individually1.

# Define a numeric vector
another_vec <- c(1, 10, 100)

# Apply the sine function element-wise
sin(another_vec)

[1]  0.8414710 -0.5440211 -0.5063656


A unexpected behavior in R:

c(3, 2 , 1) + c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)

Warning in c(3, 2, 1) + c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5): longer object length is not a
multiple of shorter object length


[1] 4 4 4 7 7


R still performs addition even though the two vectors are not of equal length, although it issues a warning. Such an operation is not defined in standard mathematics.

title: 37  Vector and matrix operation
text: Not all functions are vectorized↩︎

title: 38  Data frame
text:
Formal
The previous chapters mirrors mathematical concepts in programming, such as vectors, matrices, logical and numeric values, and matrix operations. This chapter transitions from mathematical structures to the more flexible requirements of data science. The data frame was developed to meet these needs, and most data encountered in ecological practice are stored in this format.
A data frame stores multiple variables recorded across multiple observations. For instance, an investigator surveys 100 individuals and records name, age, and sex. The dataset consists of three columns: the first for name as character, the second for age as integer, and the third as logical (TRUE if female and FALSE if male). Similarly, a field researcher visits fifteen sites and records site name, altitude, pH, and other variables.
A data frame is a rectangular structure (similar to a matrix Chapter 5 and Chapter 36), where each column represents a variable. However, unlike a matrix, the data type of each column can differ.
Another practical advantage of a data frame is that columns typically have names, allowing access by column name rather than numerical index.
A data frame is constructed with the function data.frame().
# Construct a data frame where each argument defines a column name and its vector of values
df <- data.frame(
  name1 = vector1, # First column named name1
  name2 = vector2, # Second column named name2
  name3 = vector3  # Third column named name3
)
The constraint is that all vectors must have equal lengths; otherwise, the structure will not form a rectangle and the operation will fail.
Columns can be conveniently accessed using df$name1, which is the most common approach. Due to underlying data structures, this is equivalent to df[, 1] or df["name1"].

title: 38  Data frame
text:
Examples

Below are three styles for creating a data frame. The third approach represents standard best practice.
1- The quickest approach is to type directly each vector in the function. The code is shorter but the column names are usually a mess.

# Method 1: Data frame created without specifying column names, resulting in default, uninformative names
my_df <- data.frame(
  c(1, 2, 3),
  c("A", "X", "B"),
  c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE))
my_df

  c.1..2..3. c..A....X....B.. c.TRUE..TRUE..FALSE.
1          1                A                 TRUE
2          2                X                 TRUE
3          3                B                FALSE



A more organized approach is to contruct the vector first and then add the vector name in the function. Ideally the vector name should be information which is not the case here.


  # Method 2: Data frame created using existing vector names as column names
  col1 <- c(1, 2, 3)
  col2 <- c("A", "X", "B")
  col3 <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)

  my_df <- data.frame(col1, col2, col3)
  my_df

  col1 col2  col3
1    1    A  TRUE
2    2    X  TRUE
3    3    B FALSE



The third method assigns a column name to each vector/variable.


  # Method 3: Data frame created with explicit, descriptive variable names
  my_df <- data.frame(
    id = col1,
    letter = col2,
    male = col3)
  my_df

  id letter  male
1  1      A  TRUE
2  2      X  TRUE
3  3      B FALSE


Different manners to extract column. The first approach represents standard best practice but can only extract one column. The remaning approach allows to extract more columns1

# Extract a column using the dollar sign ($) operator (returns a vector)
my_df$id

[1] 1 2 3

# Extract the first column using matrix-style numerical indexing (returns a vector)
my_df[, 1]

[1] 1 2 3

# Subset a column by name using single brackets (returns a 1-column data frame)
my_df["id"]

  id
1  1
2  2
3  3

# Extract a column by name using matrix-style character indexing (returns a vector)
my_df[, "id"]

[1] 1 2 3

# Extract two column by name using matrix-style character indexing (returns a 2-column data frame)
my_df[, c("id", "letter")]

  id letter
1  1      A
2  2      X
3  3      B


Appending a new column to a data frame

# Add a new column (variable) to the data frame
my_df$name <- c("Andry", "Feno", "Felana")
my_df

  id letter  male   name
1  1      A  TRUE  Andry
2  2      X  TRUE   Feno
3  3      B FALSE Felana

title: 38  Data frame
text:
Tips and warnings

Column names are considered variables and should not include spaces or special characters; the same rules apply as in Chapter 29.
In principle, all input vectors when constructing a data frame should be of equal length. There is a special case where a vector of length one is provided: R creates a constant vector matching the length of the longest vector.

# Construct a data frame using a scalar (recycled) and a multi-element vector
data.frame(constant = 1, letters = c("A", "B", "C"))

  constant letters
1        1       A
2        1       B
3        1       C


A tibble is a common variation of the data frame structure. The popular package ecosystem tidyverse prefers data formatted as a tibble, but standard data frames also work. The differences are subtle enough that either format can be used in most workflows.
A character vector is often converted into a factor (see last tip in Chapter 35).
The basic concepts above are useful for understanding the core structure and goals of this volume. However, manual entry is not the ideal method for entering data into R. Most often, data are entered in spreadsheet software such as Excel and subsequently imported into R as a data frame.

title: 38  Data frame
text: With dplyr, selecting columns is done with the function select↩︎

title: 39  List
text:
Formal
A list is the most flexible object for storing data. Following the building metaphor, a vector (Chapter 35) represents a tall building where every floor contains identical units, such as single-bedroom apartments, while a matrix (Chapter 36) represents a building with multiple identical units on each floor. In contrast, a list is like a multistory building where each floor can serve an entirely different purpose.
For instance, the first floor can be a swimming pool, the second floor a library, the third floor three separate apartments, and the fifth floor an entire secondary multistory building.
While such a building is unrealistic in architecture, it highlights the extreme flexibility of lists. Translating this back to programming, each list element must consist of data types introduced earlier. For instance, the first element of a list can be a character vector, the second a single numeric value, the third a matrix, and the fourth another list.
As a consequence, lists are not designed for direct mathematical calculations and can be non-trivial to manipulate because they lack a uniform rectangular structure.
A list is constructed with the function list().
# Construct a list where each argument defines an element name and its associated R object
my_list <- list(
  name1 = object1, # First element containing object1
  name2 = object2, # Second element containing object2
  name3 = object3  # Third element containing object3
)
Unlike matrices or data frames, there are no structural constraints on the types or dimensions of the stored objects; elements may consist of vectors of varying lengths, matrices, data frames, or other lists.
Objects can be accessed directly using double square brackets [[]], for instanmce my_list[[1]] or my_list[["name1"]], which extract the underlying object. If the elements are named, my_list$name1 can also be used as a convenient shortcut.
Single square brackets my_list[1] or my_list["name1"] subset the structure, returning a smaller list containing the specified element rather than the object itself.

title: 39  List
text:
Examples

# Construct a list containing numeric, list, and matrix objects
silly_example <- list(
  mine = 1,                              # First element: single numeric value
  list(yours = c(1, 2), hers = "A"),     # Second element: unnamed nested list
  mat = matrix(1:6, nrow = 2)            # Third element: 2x3 numeric matrix
)


Unlike a vector or a matrix, a list is displayed differently when printed.

# Print the complete list object to observe its hierarchical output structure
silly_example

$mine
[1] 1

[[2]]
[[2]]$yours
[1] 1 2

[[2]]$hers
[1] "A"


$mat
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    3    5
[2,]    2    4    6


Extracting one element: double vs. single bracket

# Extract the value of the first element
silly_example[[1]]

[1] 1

str(silly_example[[1]])

 num 1

# Subset the list to include only the first element
silly_example[1]

$mine
[1] 1

str(silly_example[1])

List of 1
 $ mine: num 1


Comparing the output reveals that double brackets ([[1]]) extract the underlying value directly, whereas single brackets ([1]) return a sublist containing the target element (indicated by $mine in the output). This structural difference can be verified using the str() function.
Extracting named elements and nested components

# Extract the named element "xx"
silly_example$mine

[1] 1

# Extract the 2nd element
silly_example[[2]]

$yours
[1] 1 2

$hers
[1] "A"

# Subset the 1st element within the 2nd element
silly_example[[2]][1]

$yours
[1] 1 2

# Extract component x from the nested list using its name
silly_example[[2]]$yours

[1] 1 2

# Extract component x from the nested list using double brackets
silly_example[[2]][[1]]

[1] 1 2

# Extract the 2nd column of the matrix stored as the 3rd element
silly_example[[3]][, 2]

[1] 3 4

title: 39  List
text:
Tips and warnings
Lists are rarely constructed manually unless specific requirements arise, such as building custom objects or tailored data structures. However, understanding list construction helpl accessing and manipulating the outputs of statistical analyses.

title: 40  Function
text:
Formal
A function in programming can be viewed as a generalization of mathematical functions (Chapter 8). This generalization makes programming exceptionally useful and powerful: the input (or independent variable) can be any data type, the number of arguments can be expanded as needed, and the output follows the same flexibility.
In R, a function can represent a simple mathematical operation (such as sin(), cos(), exp(), or log()), a data constructor (such as c(), matrix(), or list()), or a summary statistic (such as mean() to compute the arithmetic average). Functions exist for nearly every statistical test, figure creation, data manipulation procedure, and tools to solve equations.
When R is installed and launched, approximately 4,250 functions are immediately available. Because these base functions do not cover every specialized workflow, new functions are created continuously.
Packages are collections of functions designed to perform specific tasks; popular examples include ggplot2 for plotting graphics and vegan for community ecological analyses. Packages streamline quantitative workflows, and the vast package ecosystem represents one of R’s primary strengths.
While the exact total number of functions across all repositories is unquantified, assuming an average of 15 functions per package yields at least 379250 functions.
Functions provide powerful capabilities, but they can also present significant challenges: how to locate the required function, how to supply appropriate arguments, how to interpret output structures, and how to resolve errors.
A function is defined using the syntax function().
# Define a function specifying its required and optional arguments
function_name <- function(argument1, argument2 = TRUE, ...) {
  # Code block executing operations using the provided arguments
  output <- argument1 + argument2 # Example computation
  return(output)
}
A function definition consists of several structural components:

title: 40  Function
text:
Function name: An identifier assigned to the function, adhering to the standard variable naming rules outlined in Chapter 29.
Assignment operator (<-) and keyword: The operator assigns the function object created by function() to the chosen name.
Arguments: Variables listed inside the parentheses, separated by commas. These accept input values passed when the function is called, and may include default values (e.g., argument2 = TRUE).
Code block: The executable statements enclosed within curly braces {} that perform operations on the input arguments.
Return output: The return() statement, which explicitly specifies the final result or object output by the function.

title: 40  Function
text:
Examples

Here are examples of basic mathematical functions:

# Calculate the sine of 1 radian
sin(1)

[1] 0.841471

# Calculate the absolute value of a negative number
abs(-2)

[1] 2

# Calculate the square root of 25
sqrt(25)

[1] 5

# Combine function outputs and store the result using assignment
result <- sqrt(25) + abs(-2)
result

[1] 7


Data manipulation

# Sort a numeric vector in ascending order
sort(c(10, 2, 4, 2, 3.1))

[1]  2.0  2.0  3.1  4.0 10.0

# Sort a numeric vector in descending order
sort(c(10, 2, 4, 2, 3.1), decreasing = TRUE)

[1] 10.0  4.0  3.1  2.0  2.0

# Sort a character vector in alphabetical order
sort(c("jaojoby", "tovo j'hay", "bessa", "reko"))

[1] "bessa"      "jaojoby"    "reko"       "tovo j'hay"

# Extract unique elements from a numeric vector, removing duplicate values
unique(c(10, 2, 4, 2, 3.1))

[1] 10.0  2.0  4.0  3.1


Plotting functions

# Generate a discrete sequence of integer values from 1 to 5
indpt_variable <- 1:5

# Compute dependent values by squaring the independent variable
dpt_variable <- indpt_variable^2

# Create a scatter plot with blue triangle markers
plot(
  x = indpt_variable, # Numeric vector of x-axis values
  y = dpt_variable,   # Numeric vector of y-axis values
  col = "blue",        # Point color
  pch = 2,             # Point symbol shape (2 = open triangle)
  type = "p"           # Plot type ("p" for points)
)








Modifying plot aesthetics.1

# Generate a discrete sequence of integer values from 1 to 5
indpt_variable <- 1:5

# Compute dependent values by squaring the independent variable
dpt_variable <- indpt_variable^2

# Create a line plot with a red line
plot(
  x = indpt_variable, # Numeric vector of x-axis values
  y = dpt_variable,   # Numeric vector of y-axis values
  col = "red",         # Line color
  type = "l"           # Plot type ("l" for lines)
)

title: 40  Function
text:
Tips and warnings

By convention, function names in R are written in lowercase. However, the naming conventions outlined in Chapter 29 are also widely applied, such as snake_case (e.g., read_csv()) or camelCase (e.g., makeMatrix()). Additionally, many foundational functions in base R utilize a period.separated naming style, such as data.frame() or read.csv().
Functions are distinguished visually and syntactically from variables by the trailing parentheses () that follow their name. While a variable stores an object, a function represents an executable action that accepts arguments within those parentheses.
The vast majority of R packages are hosted on CRAN (Comprehensive R Archive Network), the official repository that subjects packages to rigorous quality and installation checks. Other major public repositories include Bioconductor, which specializes in genomic and biological data analyses, and GitHub, which hosts developmental versions and user-contributed community packages.
Despite the large number of functions in R, a user ultimately has specific needs and it is more efficient to write a function. That’s when programming becomes more and more fun.


Bonus
The matrix() function (Chapter 36) illustrates two core principles of function construction: implicit versus explicit arguments, and arguments with versus without default values.
Inspecting the documentation for the matrix() function reveals its formal function signature and argument list:






Figure 40.1: Definition of the arguments for the function matrix()



The function defines four primary arguments: data, nrow, ncol, and byrow.
Implicit vs explicit argument names
Consider the fruit data used in this handbook. The matrix was constructed by specifying argument names explicitly within the function call.

# Define a numeric vector of fruit counts
data_fruit <- c(6, 3, 0, 1, 3, 1, 10, 0, 0.5, 0, 0, 2)

# Construct a 4x3 matrix using explicit argument names in standard order
mat <- matrix(
  data = data_fruit,
  nrow = 4,
  ncol = 3,
  byrow = FALSE
)
mat

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    6    3  0.5
[2,]    3    1  0.0
[3,]    0   10  0.0
[4,]    1    0  2.0


In the next example below, the order of the arguments was shuffled but that does not affect the output. It works because the argument names are explicitly supplied.

# Construct a matrix using explicit argument names in arbitrary order
mat <- matrix(
  byrow = FALSE, # byrow is provided first
  ncol = 3,
  data = data_fruit,
  nrow = 4
)
mat

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    6    3  0.5
[2,]    3    1  0.0
[3,]    0   10  0.0
[4,]    1    0  2.0


In the next example, the argument names are omitted. Passing values without supplying explicit names relies on implicit (positional) arguments. In positional matching, R assigns input values based strictly on the order defined in the function’s formal specification.

# Construct a matrix using positional matching (data, nrow, ncol, byrow)
mat <- matrix(data_fruit, 4, 3, FALSE)
mat

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    6    3  0.5
[2,]    3    1  0.0
[3,]    0   10  0.0
[4,]    1    0  2.0


Reordering positional values can result in unintended behaviors or runtime errors. A frequent source of errors is a mismatch between the expected position of an argument and the position of the value provided2.

# Alter dimensions by swapping positional arguments for nrow and ncol
mat <- matrix(data_fruit, 3, 4, FALSE)
mat

     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
[1,]    6    1 10.0    0
[2,]    3    3  0.0    0
[3,]    0    1  0.5    2



# Attempt to pass matrix dimensions before data, resulting in a strange behavior
mat <- matrix(3, data_fruit, 4, FALSE)
mat

     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
[1,]    3    3    3    3
[2,]    3    3    3    3
[3,]    3    3    3    3
[4,]    3    3    3    3
[5,]    3    3    3    3
[6,]    3    3    3    3


Using explicit argument names avoids this issue entirely or/and the challenge of remembering the order of each argument. However, in cases where the function’s first argument is self-evident, it is often supplied implicitly, with subsequent parameters remaining explicit.

# Pass the data vector implicitly while specifying remaining arguments explicitly
mat <- matrix(
  data_fruit,
  nrow = 4,
  ncol = 3,
  byrow = FALSE)

Default argument values

Specifying all arguments explicitly:


# Construct a matrix with all arguments defined explicitly
mat <- matrix(
  data = data_fruit,
  nrow = 4,
  ncol = 3,
  byrow = FALSE
)
mat

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    6    3  0.5
[2,]    3    1  0.0
[3,]    0   10  0.0
[4,]    1    0  2.0



Omitting arguments with default values:

When optional arguments are omitted, R uses their predefined default values. If ncol is not specified, it is automatically inferred from the length of the data vector and nrow. The byrow parameter defaults to FALSE.

# Construct a matrix using default values for ncol and byrow
mat <- matrix(
  data = data_fruit,
  nrow = 4
)
mat

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    6    3  0.5
[2,]    3    1  0.0
[3,]    0   10  0.0
[4,]    1    0  2.0


Default argument values simplify function calls. For example, plotting functions contain over 20 optional arguments, such as point color (col) or character size (cex). Default values eliminate the need to specify every parameter explicitly when standard behavior is desired.

title: 41  Pseudocode
text:
Formal
The primary tenet of evolution is that natural selection has acted over a sufficiently long period that organisms have become better adapted to their environment. Traits of present-day organisms represent a collection of solutions to challenges that their ancestors faced. Evolution has produced organisms that excel at solving problems, to the extent that humans look to nature (e.g., for medicine) to solve human challenges.
Programming has existed since the birth of computers. With nearly 180 years of evolution1, programmers have faced numerous challenges that led to the development of vast coding practices designed to surmount these issues. For ecologists and data scientists, adopting some of these practices can also make coding easier. One practice that is almost never mentioned in applied coding is the use of pseudocode.
While the majority of readers of this book might not need to develop pseudocode in the traditional programmer sense, a accessible version—referred to here as pseudo-pseudocode—can be added to programming toolkits. In a nutshell, pseudo-pseudocode is a written description or sketch that could be shown to a colleague or relative to explain how the code is structured and what the code is doing.
Pseudocode is an informal, high-level way of writing computer program algorithms using plain, human-readable language mixed with basic programming concepts. It allows developers to outline logic and program structure without worrying about strict syntax rules, semicolons, or memory management.
The key characteristics of a pseudocode are:

title: 41  Pseudocode
text:
Human-Readable: Written in plain English (or any natural language) so both technical and non-technical stakeholders can understand it.
Syntax-Free: Has no rigid compilation rules or syntax errors.
Language-Agnostic: Translates easily into any actual programming language like Python, JavaScript, Java, or C++.
Structure-Oriented: Uses familiar programming structures like loops, conditionals, and functions to maintain logical flow.

title: 41  Pseudocode
text:
Examples

The example below is a developper style of the pseudocode is to find and print the largest of two numbers.
BEGIN
    READ number1
    READ number2

    IF number1 > number2 THEN
        PRINT "number1 is greater"
    ELSE IF number2 > number1 THEN
        PRINT "number2 is greater"
    ELSE
        PRINT "Both numbers are equal"
    ENDIF
END

An example of pseudo-pseudocode from the pseudocode above

Import or input two variables called number1 and number2
Compare the values (three possible scenarios)
Print to the console which scenario occurred

A more concrete example of pseudo-pseudocode to plot a linear regression between the height and width of trees

Import data containing the two columns
Clean the data if needed
Rename the columns to height and width
Perform a linear regression and extract the regression coefficient, the intercept, and the adjusted R2
Create the scatterplot, add the regression line, and add an inset in the top-left showing the equation y = ax + b (with a and b replaced by their estimated values) alongside the adjusted R2
Export the plot as a PDF file

title: 41  Pseudocode
text:
Tips and warnings

Pseudo-pseudocode is not an official term; it is used in this chapter to illustrate an idea.
Pseudocode consists of brainstorming and constructing the skeleton of the code before actually writing any code.
Pseudo-pseudocode can be implemented in many ways. The most practical approach is to treat pseudo-pseudocode as the comments that will appear in the future code—writing comments is strongly advised.
There are many ways to reach the same result. For instance, while most figures are created using ggplot2, all figures in this volume use base R. Thinking at a higher level provides a clear conceptual understanding of the process rather than focusing strictly on specific syntax or functions.
Pseudocode is an effective format for sharing workflow logic with colleagues or advisors.

title: 42  Debugging
text:
Formal
Studies on software quality show that industry-standard code contains 10 to 50 bugs per 1,000 lines of written code. This means about one error every 20 to 67 lines. Thus, even professionally trained programmers make mistakes. As the proverb says: “Mihinam-bary aza misy latsaka”
Bugs are inevitable at any skill level. For most readers, bugs are primarily execution errors in code. The emotional dissonance between expecting final results and receiving a rejection message from the program can make encountering an error feel crushing.
Bugs made by beginner programmers and software engineers are not of the same nature. Most bugs created by beginners can be circumvented through the proper use of an IDE (Chapter 28) and better grasp of the basic principles, whereas advanced programmers rely on debugging tools (also included in IDEs). However, software engineers were also beginner programmers once. As with any learning process, the initial phase is the hardest and slowest1. While encountering a bug is annoying, debugging can also be enjoyable—much like solving a puzzle.
A bug is an error, flaw, or fault in a computer program that causes it to produce an incorrect, unexpected, or unintended result. Bugs can stem from syntactic mistakes (such as typos or missing parentheses), semantic issues (such as passing an incorrect data type to an argument), or logical errors (where the code executes without failing but returns mathematically or conceptually incorrect output).
Debugging is the systematic process of identifying, isolating, and resolving bugs within software code. It involves analyzing error messages, stepping through code execution line by line, inspecting variable values in the working environment, and testing fixes to ensure the program behaves as intended.

title: 42  Debugging
text:
Examples

Object not found: Typo in the variable name

# Define a numeric variable storing the value 1
variable1 <- 1

# Square variable1, resulting in an error due to a typo (varable1)
variable_squared <- varable1^2

Error: object 'varable1' not found


Object not found: Some preceeding lines were not executed. As seen in the error message, the object b is not found. Indeed, inspecting the environment reveals that no object b was created. A closer inspection of the console history shows that the execution ran a followed directly by c <- a + b and skipped creating b.






Figure 42.1: Object not found



Improper argument: The error below is caused by a type mismatch: the value is stored as a character string rather than a numeric value, whereas the argument for sin() must be of numeric type.

# Storing a value 1
value <- "1"

# Taking the sine
sin(value)

Error in sin(value): non-numeric argument to mathematical function


Structural problem: a matrix multiplication (Chapter 7 Chapter 37) fails below because the matrix dimension requirements are not satisfied.


# # Define a matrix representing the quantity of fruit purchased per person (4 rows, 3 columns)
mat <-
    matrix(c(6, 3, 0, 1, 3, 1, 10, 0, 0.5, 0, 0, 2),
    nrow = 4,
    ncol = 3)
mat

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    6    3  0.5
[2,]    3    1  0.0
[3,]    0   10  0.0
[4,]    1    0  2.0

# Define a numeric vector representing the price of 4 fruit items
price <- c(500, 1000, 2000, 600)

# Expenditure per person (fails because inner dimensions 4x3 and 4x1 do not conform)
mat %*% price

Error in mat %*% price: non-conformable arguments

title: 42  Debugging
text:
Tips and warnings

“You made a mistake.” For beginner and even intermediate coders, encountering an error message often causes frustration, hinting that there might be something wrong with the program. However, it is usually a human mistake.
It is often easier to spot errors in someone else’s code than in one’s own. This makes sense and applies to everyday life as well. If stuck, stepping away for a while allows one to return to the code with a fresh perspective.
Read the error message carefully and attempt to understand it. With sufficient repetition and practice, the source of an error becomes obvious.
Run the code line by line. Identifying an error when executing multiple lines at once is difficult; running code sequentially makes it easier to pinpoint where the issue occurred.
Every time a function is called, ensure the required arguments, argument data types, and expected output types are clearly understood.
IDEs (Chapter 28) are powerful tools that help prevent simple mistakes:

Auto-suggestion: Once a variable or function exists in the workspace, typing the full name manually is unnecessary.
Auto-completion of parentheses to prevent mismatched brackets.
Real-time syntax checking to flag simple typos instantaneously.
Additional helper features.

Warnings are not errors. They may sometimes be safely ignored, but they can also indicate underlying issues that cause problems in subsequent lines.
Actual bugs within R or R packages can occur, but such claims must be supported with reproducible evidence before reporting them to developers.
The absence of an error message does not guarantee that the code is behaving as intended.
